Name: Dax Kilby
Report:
Kilby ranked 23rd on our 2025 Draft Board thanks to his projectable 6-foot-2 frame and excellent contact performance on the showcase circuit. He was selected 39th overall by the Yankees and given a bonus just shy of $2.8 million to eschew a commitment to Clemson. After the draft, he looked meaningfully better on defense (which vaulted him into the 50 FV tier) and went on a tear at the plate, though in too small a sample to care much about. The late-season surge made Kilby a scouting focal point entering 2026, but a hamstring issue cost him most of the season. He didn't start playing regularly until late July and ended the regular season with 32 games at Low-A Tampa, the same level he'd crushed the year prior. Needing reps and a more advanced challenge, the Yankees sent Kilby to the Arizona Fall League, where he thrived for the first several weeks and cooled off late. 
For a hitter as big and rangy as Kilby is, his swing is exceptionally short. He lacks precise barrel feel and doesn't make a ton of flush, squared-up contact, but his bat is on plane with the baseball for a long time and he naturally covers a good bit of the strike zone, especially the inner half. He's apt to swing over the top of well-executed sinking stuff near the bottom of the zone. It's tough to get a quantifiable feel for Kilby's contact skill because his entire career, dating all the way back to the high school showcase circuit, is just one relatively small-sample chunk after another. His 76% contact rate during the 2026 regular season is the worst of those chunks, though it's still in line with the big league average. Though Kilby's feel to hit is pretty average visually, his performance has been consistently above. Combine that with roughly average raw power that should improve as Kilby matures, and he has a chance to be an above-average contact hitter with above-average power. 
That'd be enough for him to profile as an everyday player virtually anywhere in the field; in Kilby's case, it will likely be at shortstop. Though he isn't especially fleet of foot, Kilby can bend, and he has soft hands and sufficient arm strength for the position. His regular season tape was better than his AFL look, and we're basing his long-term shortstop projection on that. If his power actualizes, his prospect stock could take a Gunnar Henderson-esque turn at some point during the next 18 months.

Name: Eric Hartman
Report:
We write about 2,000 prospect profiles per year, and if you had to line those players up in the order by which their 2026 production deviated from expectation, Hartman might just lead the bunch. A guy who once projected as a fourth outfielder with work to do on both sides of the ball blossomed into a potential building block, and now my prior assessment that “Hartman isn't likely to grow into a ton of power” is in line for a table at Freezing Cold Takes. Let’s take a look at how we got from A to B and, if we're still feeling bold, take a gander at what C might look like down the road.
Hartman was an overslot pick out of an Alberta high school in 2024. Despite the cold-weather background, he worked his way into the Low-A lineup in short order and had a productive, if speed-centric, debut season in Augusta. At that point, he was a groundball hitter with 40 measurable power. A year later, Hartman’s max exit velocity climbed from 108 to 113 mph, his EV90 increased from 102 to 105, and his launch angle rose from 10 to 17 degrees. It came with a sharp reduction in his groundball rate and only a modest uptick in swing-and-miss (though he whiffed more often after a promotion to Double-A), not to mention a tidy 133 wRC+ at High-A.
The obvious change year over year is that Hartman got much more physical, and, not surprisingly, his bat looked a heck of a lot quicker. His other adjustments were more ephemeral. His hand placement varied throughout the course of the year, with a corresponding change in the length of his load. But that was true in 2025 as well, as was his tendency to pull the ball. The story here is that Hartman got bigger, got better at catching the ball out front, and traded a bunch of rollover grounders for long homers. That doesn’t make him a hitter without risk. He’s often front-footed by secondaries, his whiff rate against sliders in particular surged at Double-A, and you could argue he’s trying to pull the ball too often. But even if Hartman proves to be a power-over-hit player, he projects to do enough damage to make it all work.
Hartman wasn't a sure thing in center to begin with, and the additional size, combined with fair feel for the outfield, seems likely to land him in a corner. He played exclusively in left after he was promoted to Double-A, and it wasn't out of deference to other top prospects competing for reps up the middle. He still moves pretty well, though, and with a little growth in his reads and routes, he should play a decent corner outfield. Regardless, the bat will determine his ultimate role. He projects as a solid regular in a corner with All-Star, middle-of-the-order upside if his feel for contact grows alongside his power. As a cold-weather player who reached Double-A as a 20-year-old, time is very much on his side.

Name: JoJo Parker
Report:
The eighth overall pick in the 2025 draft, Parker looks like a well-rounded future contributor. After a solid, if unspectacular, start to his career in Dunedin, the Mississippi native tore the cover off the ball in June and soon after earned a promotion to High-A Vancouver. There, he hit .316/.443/.418 with almost as many walks as strikeouts, and was an energetic sparkplug down the stretch as he helped lead the Canadians to the Northwest League title.
Parker offers a little bit of everything at the plate. He has a lovely connected swing with above-average bat speed, and the way he’s able to rip his hands through the zone and get the barrel ahead of an inside pitch gives me confidence that he'll be able to handle big league velocity without any trouble. His 43% hard-hit rate is great for any A-baller and fantastic for guy who played most of the season as a 19-year-old. Parker has average power already, and while he’s not overly projectable, there should be at least a little more coming. If there’s a nitpick here, it’s that he’s on the passive side: His swing rate was under 40% and his chase rate jumps when he has two strikes. Nobody’s perfect, though, and ultimately Parker’s blend of contact, power, and on-base skill justifies the lofty hit projections.
Defensively, Parker does a few things well at short. He has a reliable pair of hands, he gets the ball out quickly, and his instincts look pretty sharp on video. He has enough arm strength, and while he'll occasionally misfire, I’m not too concerned about his accuracy either. He doesn't have a ton of range, though, and he doesn't have the lithe build that suggests he’s going to grow into more. You can see a fit as a reliability-over-range shortstop early in his career, but he’s already played a little at third, and I think that’s where he'll ultimately wind up. Regardless, Parker is on the fast track. Whether he returns to Vancouver at the start of 2027 or not, he’s going to spend most of the year at the upper levels, and the 2028 ETA almost feels like a conservative projection.

Name: Tate Southisene
Report:
The Braves had a long gap between their first pick in the 2025 draft and their second. They decided to spread the money around, so when they grabbed Southisene at no. 22, it was a haircut selection of a high-variance athlete with middle-of-the-diamond projection but less certainty at the plate than you normally see at that spot in the draft. A rough beginning to pro ball — 27 strikeouts, one walk, no homers in 66 plate appearances — suggested a long road ahead. Instead, Southisene now looks like a case study in not panicking about those late-season, post-draft cameos. In year two, Southisene dominated Low-A, then posted a 121 wRC+ in 38 games at High-A. He was quickly promoted to Double-A, but an errant fastball broke his hand and ended his season in his first game at the level. Back for the Arizona Fall League, Southisene looked good at the plate, if rusty on defense.
Southisene is a plus athlete and runner. He’s twitchy and has good body control, which shows up both in his movements when he’s running or on defense, and at the plate. In addition to the athleticism, Southisene has shown aptitude as well. His 2026 breakout was keyed by a few swing alterations: He changed his setup at the plate, quieted some of his mechanics, and shortened his bat path. The cumulative effect is that he was able to make a decent rate of contact — 74%, 81% in the zone — while still tapping into his power, which is comfortably average already. You’d like to see even more contact as he matures, but this was a big step in the right direction.
Here at FanGraphs, we often write about reliability-over-range defenders, guys who are valuable even if they aren't especially flashy because they turn every ordinary grounder into a low-drama out. Southisene’s tape is the opposite of that. He’s capable of making fantastic, diving plays. He can range deep into the six hole and fire a strike to first, and he’s able to run down popups and short flares that even good big league shortstops wouldn't quite wrangle. 
But Southisene doesn't always dot the i’s and cross the t’s. His approach to routine grounders can get casual, his throwing mechanics look worse when he has a lot of time to think, and his accuracy was not very good this past summer. Evaluators are mixed on where he belongs long-term. Some see second as a possibility, and of course his speed gives him a lot of upside in center. I'm still projecting him at short for now, as the good stuff he does there is very good, and he’s still relatively new to the position (his older brother soaked up a lot of reps at short when they were in high school together). Regardless of where he winds up, Southisene has the speed and range to make an impact.

Name: Carlos Lagrange
Report:
Lagrange (pronounced "la-GRAWN-hey") had walk-prone rookie ball campaigns in 2022 and 2023, then worked just 29.2 frames (including a Fall League stint) in 2024 due to bouts of lower back inflammation. He entered 2025 as a prospect with enormous stuff and an exciting ceiling, but a sketchy track record of health and on-field performance. Then he went out and logged a surprising 120 innings, mostly at Double-A Somerset. A better-conditioned Lagrange held upper-90s velo for the entirety of that slate, and threw much of his four-pitch arsenal for strikes more reliably than he ever had before, though still not at a starter's clip. In 2026, the right-hander moved to the bullpen at the beginning of June before injuring his shoulder capsule at the end of it. He missed two and half months, but was sitting 100 when he returned in mid-September for one last outing. 
Though he has the repertoire depth to be a starter, Lagrange's health and strike-throwing track record have led to a bullpen projection for a while here at FanGraphs. The headliner of his arsenal is his radar-gun-testing fastball, which peaks at 103 mph. It has overwhelmed minor league hitters, who both chased and missed it just shy of 30% of the time in 2026. He can throw both of his breaking balls for strikes more reliably, especially a 88-92 mph slider that might otherwise be classified as a cutter were it not 10 mph slower than his fastball. He'll back door his slider or a slower 82-86 mph sweeper (listed as the curveball here; neither of Lagrange's breakers have negative vertical movement) against lefties, and then finish them with either elevated fastballs or an increasingly nasty 90-mph changeup. His attack against righties is less robust, limited to in-zone sliders and elevated fastballs, as Lagrange doesn't have good feel for locating his breaking stuff off the plate for chase. He had pronounced reverse splits in 2026 because of this. These are small blemishes that, when mixed with below-average control, led to some bumpy innings throughout Lagrange's starts, but as a single-inning power reliever, they'll be less consequential. Even with David Bednar back in the fold, Lagrange might have an opportunity to slide into the very back of the Yankees' bullpen early in 2027. He'll probably stay there for a while.

Name: Johnny King
Report:
King signed for second-round money in the 2024 draft to forgo his commitment to Miami. Similar to his pro debut, the lefty’s 2026 campaign was in many ways dominant (3.16 ERA, 30.5% strikeout rate, 0.68 HR/9, unhittable breaking ball), though again with more walks than you’d expect from a guy with good stuff and a decent delivery. Still, it was a positive year overall. King was a trendy breakout pick last winter, and now that he’s proved his stuff works against mid-to-high-level minor league competition, he'll enter 2027 with an outside chance to work big league innings.
King has a prototypical starter’s build and athleticism, with a strong lower half and a clean arm circle. He'll occasionally overthrow, and a significant heel grind can get him off balance, but there’s otherwise a lot to like in his delivery. He raised his arm slot a tick this year, which led to subtle differences in how his pitches moved, though not really how they performed; better hitters made slightly more contact, but the arsenal still grades well. He generates plus extension, and his drop-and-drive delivery helps his carrying, mid-90s fastball play well up in the zone. He pairs the heater with a long, sharp slider that flashes plus and a fading change that flashes above average. While still inconsistent — King doesn’t use it much and would perhaps benefit from dusting it off a little more often — the cambio took a step forward year over year. For all the walks, King will sometimes show feel to pitch that's mature beyond his years, adding and subtracting on a back door breaking ball, or surgically dotting the fastball at the top of the zone against guys who can't get the barrel there.
There are risks here. King has the delivery, and at times has shown the command, to start, but the overall volume of strikes has lagged. His change isn't a finished product, and there’s a chance his current breaking ball isn’t sharp enough to reliably miss big league bats. Still, there aren't many 20-year-old lefties with this kind of arm talent. The change should improve, and he may yet add a power breaking ball as he matures. There are enough ingredients here to project him as a mid-rotation starter, and with this update, he enters our Top 100 list.

Name: Cam Caminiti
Report:
Caminiti, the cousin of the late Ken Caminiti, was a two-way star in high school even as his future was clearly on the mound. He signed for $3.5 million out of a Scottsdale high school and has quickly grown into one of the top left-handed pitching prospects in baseball. He notched a 3.38 ERA with a 25.8% strikeout rate and a 47% groundball rate across two levels in 2026, and made his Double-A debut a couple of days before his 20th birthday.
Caminiti is a great athlete who repeats his delivery well. He pitches from the stretch and has a high leg kick, a long stride, and a crossfire motion. He has a clean arm swing and landing, both of which give him a great control foundation. His fastball command has long been advanced for his age, and still is: He can land the fastball to both sides of the plate and has good feel for elevating it. As was the case 12 months ago, Caminiti can touch the upper 90s but tends to sit 92-95, and, if anything, he was on the lower end of that band by year’s end. That makes him reliant on command and angle, as the velo and shape are otherwise ordinary. His slot on the fastball is a couple of inches higher than on his breaking stuff. So far, hitters haven’t punished him for it, but it’s a looming concern.
Caminiti’s secondary stuff often looks average to the eye, but it plays better than that. His slider is fairly long with average spin, and while it doesn't look sharp, lefties in particular have a tough time holding up. His fading change has good action and draws more chases than anything else in the holster, though he slows his body down a bit and is prone to missing uncompetitively to the arm side. It’s worth remembering that he’s only 20, and that there’s a lot of runway for him to get better at executing the best versions of these pitches.
Entering 2026, we thought long and hard about putting Caminiti on the Top 100. Ultimately, we decided that we wanted to see him hold his stuff deeper into games — he'd thrown just 70 frames in 2025 — and ideally show progress with his secondaries and control. Two out of three isn’t bad, as the change started to flash more often and he worked 114.2 very solid innings. And even though he again walked about 11% of hitters, Caminiti’s athleticism and clean delivery leave us optimistic he'll grow there as well. With this update, he enters our Top 100.

Name: Elmer Rodríguez
Report:
Originally a Red Sox prospect, Rodríguez enjoyed a two-tick velo spike in 2024, was traded to the Yankees for Carlos Narváez that winter, and has been able to sustain mid-90s heat across a starter's load of innings for each of the last two seasons. He spent most of 2026 at Triple-A Scranton, where he posted a 2.45 ERA, but labored through a six-start, 5.40-ERA cup of coffee in the majors. 
Rodríguez will pitch his way in and out of jams, as he's been fairly walk-prone but often bails himself out by generating a double-play ball; his sinker had a 61% groundball rate in 2026. Like Will Warren and Michael King before him, Rodríguez has a bit of a cross-bodied delivery and a three-quarters arm slot that helps him play X-games with his sinker and a two-planed curveball, which he can tweak to have more of a sweeper shape; the curveball generated a plus-plus miss rate in 2026. A cutter and changeup that both average 88 mph give him a full mix that finishes in all four quadrants of the zone, but in part because he lacks great command, neither of those pitches is especially nasty or consistent right now. If either is to outpace this projection in terms of performance, it will likely be thanks to Elmer also improving his command beyond what I forecast here. He had far too many walk-prone starts in 2026, which shortened many of his outings. He only worked six or more innings four times all year and is going to have a hard time cracking the Yankees' rotation until that improves. This might simply mean throwing more sinkers, which Rodríguez threw for strikes at a 67% clip in 2026, and accepting fewer strikeouts as a cost of working deeper into games. 
There's a little less polish on Rodríguez than most other upper-level performers on 40-man rosters, but the quality of his sinker and breaking ball give him no. 4 starter projection despite these potentially frustrating issues.

Name: Nolan Perry
Report:
Perry was the clear breakout prospect in Toronto’s system in 2026. Originally drafted in 2022, the righty signed for a modest $200,000 bonus. He spent his first pro season on the complex and his second walking nearly 20% of opposing hitters in Low-A. He then had TJ, which prematurely ended his 2024 campaign and kept him out for all of the following year as well. 
Upon his return, Perry looked like a new pitcher. His average fastball velocity jumped from 92 to 94 mph, and his breaking balls looked correspondingly sharper as well. Perhaps most surprisingly, Perry threw way more strikes. Across three levels, he allowed just 32 free passes in 82.2 innings and struck out nearly four times as many hitters as he walked. In six months, he’s leapt from an afterthought to one of this system's top pitchers. 
Perry has the easy operation of a starter. He’s a strong kid with a well-honed, high-three-quarters delivery and a clean arm swing. He'll occasionally overthrow and pull the fastball with him, but overall his command is pretty good, particularly for someone coming back from major surgery. He’s adept at keeping the fastball up in the zone and tends to locate his breaking balls in places hitters are likely to chase them. He has good feel for spin, and hitters struggle with his buckling curveball in particular. And while he doesn't have the same kind of feel for his sinking change, hitters couldn't do anything with it this year. 
While Perry looks like a starter, evaluators are split on whether he’s more of a backend or mid-rotation prospect. At his best, his stuff looks crisp enough for the latter role, and a no. 3/4 starter outcome is a realistic ceiling. But Perry’s workload has been light enough that it’s hard to say with much conviction that he'll be able to maintain that over a full season. He averaged just four innings per outing in 2026 and only topped 80 pitches twice. Between that and a lower chase rate at Double-A — Perry tends to work the edges, and it’s fair to notice that advanced hitters didn’t bite as much as low-minors opponents — there are enough question marks to keep him in this value tier for now. Were I scouting for a big league team, I’d project him as a no. 4. For us, he’s a Pick to Click and a guy we’ll monitor closely next spring for signs that he’s able to maintain his best stuff in longer bursts.

Name: Luke Sinnard
Report: Were we firing up a new dynasty on MVP Baseball and toggling off the “injuries” button in the gameplay settings, Sinnard would be the top pitcher in this system. He throws gas with extension and carry out of a high release and has unusually good feel for locating his fastball, particularly when he’s placing it above bats in the upper part of the zone. His slider and curve both flash plus, and his best splitters leave hitters to contemplate retirement on their way back to the dugout. Long-levered pitchers with a little stiffness in their movements aren't usually good rotation bets, but Sinnard’s control and command are advanced, particularly given how few reps he’s had as a professional. He’s very good. The rub here is that injuries are regrettably part of the story. He missed his junior season of college recuperating from Tommy John surgery, then threw 72.1 innings in 2025 as he battled through an elbow stress reaction. An abdominal strain put him on the shelf for several weeks in 2026, and so even though his numbers were outstanding — 2.94 ERA, 28.9% strikeout rate, 7.6% walk rate, great CSW numbers on everything in the holster and diabolical data on the split in particular — he accrued them while logging just 52 innings and averaging fewer than four frames per start. Like a bunch of other tall pitchers who throw strikes even with just fair athleticism, Sinnard looks like a candidate for the “good or unavailable” pitcher bucket. The top end of that range of outcomes is something like James Paxton’s career, with A.J. Puk in the middle, and a bunch of guys we've all forgotten about at the other extreme. In thinking through how to value Sinnard, risk is as much a part of the equation as talent. I imagine teams have a range of projections on him, which could make him an intriguing trade candidate if the win-now Braves opt to exchange upside for a little more certainty as they chase another playoff berth in 2027.

Name: Hunter Dietz
Report:
After a slow start to his college career, Dietz became one of the 2026 draft's big risers. He suffered a stress fracture in his elbow in 2023 and had a major setback the following year, which limited him to just four total appearances as an underclassman. Unshackled from the training table, Dietz produced a dominant junior season, striking out 131 batters while posting a 3.57 ERA and solid peripherals. Working with a mid-to-upper-90s fastball and a tight, upper-80s slider, the southpaw overwhelmed college bats with power stuff, and also showed he could pull the string and switch to a slower breaking ball to get hitters out on their front foot. The Yankees made him their first round pick and gave him a bonus just shy of $2.5 million, which was a tad under slot; he did not pitch at an affiliate after the draft.
Dietz is enormous, has rare velo for a lefty starter, and possesses a monster downhill slider that's aided by his size and high arm slot. He’s balanced throughout his delivery and has a clean and simple arm swing, but he isn't especially loose or twitchy. While he manages to throw plenty of strikes, he isn't precise. His relative inexperience and injury history are factors, and there could be growth ahead as he gets more reps, though he still projects as more of a “hit a region” than a “hit a spot” guy. Two issues loom large. The first is his lack of a changeup: He only threw a handful of them in college, and the pitch is understandably raw relative to the rest of the arsenal. The other is injuries, which are harder to account for. You can dream on Dietz developing into a mid-rotation, innings-eating workhorse (by modern standards, anyway), but the elbow history is awfully scary. This is a high-variance college arm who had one of the stronger arrow-up seasons across all of baseball in 2026.

Name: Cole Carlon
Report:
We had Carlon as one of the top arms on our Draft Board, but the southpaw fell to the 29th overall pick. Part of that is because the 2026 draft, particularly among the pitchers, was a jumble of eye-of-the-beholder players, and some teams may have been wary that he left one of his last starts of the year with a sore arm, which coincided with a brief velo dip down the stretch.
Carlon is a lefty starter with an XL frame. He was a reliever for most of his career at ASU before becoming the Friday guy for the Sun Devils in 2026 and blossoming into a first-round talent. Despite the size and a herky-jerky delivery that features a lot of moving parts, he throws strikes. His fastball touched triple digits at times this year and comfortably sat 93-96 mph in most outings. His primary offspeed is a plus power slider with late downward break that he can throw to both lefties and righties. He also threw an occasional curve and change, almost as if to remind scouts and draft evaluators that he has them.
Carlon’s fastball plays beneath the number, which leaves him heavily reliant on the slider. He is able to run that pitch on and off the plate with consistently sharp break and pretty good feel for moving it around the zone, which gives him a chance to start even if everything else in the holster is pedestrian. I’d put his chances of staying in the rotation at a little better than 50/50, with late-inning upside in relief.

Name: Conor Essenburg
Report:
Essenburg was an overslot, $1.2 million signee out of an Illinois high school in 2025. He was a two-way prospect as an amateur and sat 89-91 mph off the mound, but Atlanta drafted him as an outfielder, and that looks like the right call after his first pro season. Cold-weather prep bats sometimes struggle in their first exposure to professional pitching, but Essenburg torched Low-A — .286/.427/.564, 161 wRC+ with 14 homers in 59 games — and then hit well following a late-season promotion to High-A while dropping his strikeout rate considerably in Rome. 
Essenburg always had projectable power, but it showed up much faster and more emphatically than expected. On the most recent Braves list, I projected that he’d grow into 55 raw, but it’s comfortably plus already, and the kid just turned 20 and isn't done growing. The data depicts a power-over-hit skill set — 69% contact rate in 2026, 79% in zone — and while that’s true, there’s more hit skill here than the numbers imply. Essenburg picks up spin pretty well, doesn’t chase much, and can use the whole field. Both his whiff and strikeout rates fell over the course of the season, and the story of a young guy gradually growing into the game sells itself. I still expect a lot of swing and miss at maturity, as he’s an open strider with a hard, uphill swing. But you have to be a decent hitter to successfully trade contact for power, and I think Essenburg is. 
After playing a mix of center and right field in Augusta, Essenburg is just about done at the former spot. He’s slowed as he’s grown, and though he’s now not particularly quick for a right fielder, he tracks fly balls just fine, and his strong, if sometimes inaccurate, arm will likely be an asset in the long run. Still, it’s all about the bat, and the upside here is as a middle-of-the-order masher. He was in consideration for our Top 100 and will likely be one of my Picks to Click this winter.

Name: Yostin Pena
Report:
Pena is a freaky 6-foot-4 outfielder with a rocket arm and 30-homer power potential. Originally slated to sign with the Cardinals in January of 2025 for a $300,000 bonus, his verbal agreement fell through, and 11 months later, he inked a deal with the Yankees instead. Pena was a tad over 18 years old when he signed, a year and change older than the typical international amateur, and when he finally got onto a pro field in June of 2026, he set fire to DSL pitching with such ease — a .375/.457/.646 line with as many walks as strikeouts and eight homers in 37 games — that the Yankees not only promoted him in late July, but skipped him over the FCL and directly onto Low-A Tampa's roster. He terrorized the Florida State League (.423 wOBA, .359 xwOBA) during the final month of the regular season. Pena slashed .354/.431/.608 with 29 extra-base hits (14 of them homers) in 61 games between the two levels, striking out just 14.1% of the time and stealing 37 bases in 42 attempts. Yes, he was old for the DSL chunk of his season, but he was young for the Florida State League portion, which was roughly 40% of his ledger. 
Pena swings with such enormous force that he's often totally out of control and nearly falls down through his finish as his helmet flies off his head. He has a big, aggressive load that features a bit of a bat wrap, but so far this has not prevented him from being consistently on time to pull the baseball. He hit some titanic pull-side homers in 2026, including after he was promoted and facing better (but still not good) velocity. Pena has plus raw power already at age 19. He hit a ball 115 mph (his airborne max was just beneath that), and his 107.9 mph EV90 is in Samuel Basallo/Hunter Goodman/Heliot Ramos territory. 
Pena has overt 30-homer ceiling, but whether he will make enough contact to get to it is another matter. Though his K% was excellent in his debut season, his underlying data was not. A 70% contact rate and 40% chase rate (44% in the FSL, and a terrifying 50% against breaking balls) indicate Pena is a very volatile offensive player likely to strike out more in 2027 and beyond. This guy loves to swing and does so recklessly, which lower-level pitching wasn't good enough to expose. It doesn't change his potential ceiling, but it does impact the likelihood that he will reach it, as well as his ability to sustain it. 
On defense, Pena mostly played center field in 2026 but is likely a right fielder long-term. His reads and routes are crude, and he's tentative and mistake-prone fielding the baseball on the ground, but his ball skills are otherwise excellent. Once he corrects his initial read, he recovers well and is comfortable at the catch point. At his fastest, Pena runs in the mid-4.3s from home to first, which is a bit slower than most good center fielders. He's talented enough to be a really good right fielder in every respect, including his arm strength. 
This is a super fun prospect with a traditional right field profile. Pena has the tools of an eventual top-30 overall prospect and the chase/miss profile of a potential bust. Players with this kind of ceiling are quite rare, so let's value Pena with enthusiasm despite the obvious risks.

Name: Dasan Hill
Report:
Hill was Minnesota's second-rounder in 2024. An athletic lefty with arm strength and good stuff, he struggled to find the zone in his first year and a half in pro ball and was shipped to Toronto in the Jeff Hoffman deal. It was only a few starts, but he hit the box more often following the trade, and if he's able to keep the free passes somewhere near the 9.7% figure he notched in Vancouver, he has a path to our Top 100 list.
Hill was arguably the most projectable pitcher in the 2024 draft, and he's still oozing with upside. He's athletic, with good hip and shoulder separation and a loose arm, and his lanky 6-foot-5 frame still has plenty of room to get stronger. He touches the upper 90s, spins a couple of quality breaking balls, and flashes a plus change with late finish. These are top-shelf pitching ingredients, and the high-end outcomes here include things like All-Star Games and Cy Young votes.
Hill is still pretty raw, though. He's a late separator, and he doesn't always repeat his delivery, which limits his ability to execute his pitches. It's particularly notable on fastballs, which he's able to locate precisely to the arm side at times, but struggles with when trying to hit the other side of the plate. The pitches themselves aren't necessarily in their final form yet, either. He's a downhill thrower, and the angle and shape of his fastball are such that it's vulnerable in the zone. His curve can steal strikes all day long, but it's almost 20 mph slower than the fastball and has a big hump, and it too gets hit a little bit. Even his slider, which is missing bats like a plus or better offering, isn't particularly firm.
There's time for all of this to coalesce. But Hill strikes me as a guy who needs reps, and I'm a little concerned that he won't get them; he certainly hasn't gotten many thus far. This past season, he finished five innings just once, he never threw 80 pitches in an outing, and the next time he sees a hitter for a third time in a game will be his first. I really like the traits, and were I still a scout, I'd bet aggressively. For us, there are enough questions about his control, pitch shapes, and stamina to hold him in this value tier for now. He's a Pick to Click candidate and a guy I'm excited to monitor in 2027.

Name: Owen Murphy
Report:
Selected as a polished high school arm with a carrying fastball on either side of 90, Murphy needed a beat to acclimate to pro ball. It looked like improved command and secondary feel had keyed a breakout in 2024, but after seven dominant starts, he blew out. He again overwhelmed High-A hitters in his return late in 2025 and then pitched well at Triple-A in 2026, enough so that Atlanta promoted him to make a handful of appearances with the big league team. He enters 2027 with a chance to claim a spot in Atlanta’s rotation.
Murphy’s game is to pepper the edges. He’s an above-average athlete with good body control, and his loose arm and flowing delivery form the basis of a plus command projection. His fastball has 19 inches of vertical break out of a low release, which helps the pitch play ahead of its pedestrian velocity. At his best, he can work both sides of the plate and elevate the fastball for whiffs. He’s also shown an ability to locate his slider and change on and off the dish as it suits him. None of his secondaries carry the mail on their own, but the long break on the curve, darting cut on the slider, and fade on the change give Murphy a handful of looks he can throw at hitters. Good feel helps the arsenal play ahead of the sum of its parts.
While Murphy reliably threw quality strikes at Gwinnett, his command during his big league outings wasn't great. He often missed his lane with the fastball, and his feel for the curve in particular seemed to vanish entirely. He didn't have many opportunities up there, and the few he did tended to come in unusual circumstances. I'm bringing this up less as a long-term worry than as an explanation for why he struggled in Atlanta. Still, the experience highlights the importance of command for Murphy’s future. Provided his touch-and-feel shows up consistently, he looks like a near-ready backend starter.

Name: Ben Hess
Report:
Hess entered 2026 as a Pick to Click for both me and Brendan, but he failed to click and instead spent more time on the IL. Injuries have plagued Hess since amateur ball. He had a stress fracture in his back in high school and was limited to 30 career starts at Alabama due to injuries, including a flexor strain. Still, Hess' size, the fluidity of his delivery, and his power pitcher's fastball/curveball combo made him a justifiable first round pick. The Yankees felt free to accelerate the workload of a better-conditioned Hess during his 2025 pro debut, and he responded, posting a 2.50 FIP across 103.1 innings while allowing just 65 hits. In 2026, he was shut down for a month with elbow inflammation and then again in August for an outright sprain, and was only able to amass 56.2 innings. 
If there's a developmental silver lining here, it's that Hess was able to polish the movement of his cutter and sweeper, which were blending together some in 2025. He also still does the things that have made him an exciting prospect for the last couple of years. He has awesome breaking stuff and is an incredibly fluid hip-and-shoulder athlete who can power way down the mound and generate stuff-aiding extension. That said, Hess is still searching for the kind of body control and repeatability that will allow him to cut his walk rate into the single digits. He's in much better shape now than when he was in college, which theoretically gives him a better shot at finding mechanical consistency. The 2027 season will be big for Hess, as it's his 40-man roster platform year. There's still a glimmer of mid-rotation ceiling here, but Hess' injury history makes it likely he produces more like a no. 4/5 type.

Name: Ricky Tiedemann
Report:
Tiedemann made his long-awaited return to the mound in 2026, and after a quick minor league tune-up, the Jays brought him to Toronto toward the end of the year. He looked understandably rusty at times, with more non-competitive misses than you normally see in the big leagues, but he also showed the plus stuff that once made him a Top 100 prospect. He struck out eight hitters in six innings of work and missed a bunch of bats with the breaking ball in particular.
On stuff and athleticism, Tiedemann still has mid-rotation starter traits. His delivery is simple and clean, with a slight crossfire, an easy operation, and a short and loose arm stroke. A lower-slot lefty, Tiedemann touches 98 with a fastball that misses plenty of bats up in the zone. He has a plus sweeping breaking ball with sharp break, a nightmare pitch for lefties and a reliable strike generator even without the platoon advantage. He also has a change, and while it’s his third-best pitch, it too looks like it’ll be at least average with a little work.
Despite that, Tiedemann’s future role is likely in relief. Drafted in 2021, the 24-year-old has only thrown 176 pro innings and hasn’t averaged even three innings per outing since his stint in the AFL back in 2023. For a team with playoff aspirations in 2027 and theoretically plenty of rotation help on the way, he may wind up in the bullpen simply out of organizational need anyway. While a rotation outcome isn't out of the question — it’d be fascinating if a non-contender swung a trade and stretched him out — the projection here is for a late-inning reliever.

Name: Briggs McKenzie
Report:
McKenzie received the biggest bonus in Atlanta’s 2025 draft, signing for just shy of $3 million. A year of pro instruction and weight training has worked wonders, as he has filled out considerably and added a few ticks of velocity. After operating on either side of 90 mph at this time in 2025, he now sits 92-94 while touching a little higher, and he could have more growth ahead of him. 
McKenzie is an athletic and projectable lefty with a clean, if long, arm swing and a deceptive delivery. That motion helps his stuff and pitchability play up, and they're already quite good to begin with. He can move his fastball up and to both sides of the plate, and run his long and tight sweeping breaking ball on and off the dish as well. His fading change is inconsistent but flashed above average a few times during my look at him in the AFL. 
The southpaw was only in Arizona because injuries took a big bite out of his 2026 campaign. He threw just 26 innings during the regular season and at one point was on the 60-day IL with nerve irritation in his pitching elbow. While that sounds a little scary, he is back on the mound and looked no worse for wear in the Fall League. Projecting forward, McKenzie has mid-rotation traits. He has sufficient velocity and seems likely to develop the command. And while his arsenal is still a little lean, there’s plenty of time for him to add a second breaking ball or a two-seamer. While we want to see more length and durability, and perhaps another tick on the gun, before we consider bumping him onto our Top 100, I anticipate that he has another gear. He'll be a Pick to Click for me this winter.

Name: Sean Duncan
Report:
Duncan is a Canuck southpaw with prototypical size, physical projection, precocious arm strength and a promising slider. He pitched in Arizona and Florida during the spring, and was in the 92-96 mph range there, slipping toward the bottom of that range as his outings went on. His low-80s slider was harder in those outings than it was the summer before, and it had bat-missing bite and depth at times. A long arm action makes the movement on his changeup inconsistent, but for a tall, cold-weather arm like this, his stuff is in a pretty good place. 
Duncan blew out during a start in the Dominican Republic while Team Canada was on their annual spring showcase tour, and he acknowledged in June that he needed Tommy John. The Yankees used the 63rd overall pick on him and gave the Vanderbilt commit a $2.5 million bonus, about a million dollars above slot. A normal rehab schedule would have Duncan back during the latter third of 2027, in time to pitch during Instructional League. He had no. 4 starter upside before the injury.

Name: Will Brick
Report:
Despite a late draft position and limited bonus pool, Toronto managed to land both our top college starter (Cole Carlon) and our favorite high school catcher in the 2026 class. Brick was paid commensurate with his talent, not his draft position; though he was selected in the fourth round, he signed for $2.5 million, early- second-round money. Brick reclassified from the 2027 class after he hit well with Team USA at the U19 World Cup in Japan in 2025. Though we have more limited and less reliable showcase data for him because he was facing a lot of 2027 draft kids over his last two summers, the data we do have is very positive, including an 83% contact rate, which is great for a projectable 6-foot-2 catcher. He moves the barrel around the zone well, and his top hand drives his swing, giving him a shot to grow into a blend of contact and power. 
Brick is a work in progress on defense. His crouch is high and his footwork erratic, but he’s an excellent athlete with a great arm, agility, and okay receiving considering his age and inexperience. Those blemishes don't add risk to his profile so much as they probably add time to his developmental journey. He'll likely debut on the Florida complex next spring.

Name: Jensen Hirschkorn
Report: Hirschkorn signed for just shy of $4 million this past summer, which is the same bonus Atlanta gave first-rounder A.J. Gracia. You can see why the Braves value the 6-foot-7 righty as that caliber of player. Hirschkorn’s coordination for an athlete his size is remarkable. He sits 92-94 and touches higher without breaking a sweat, and he’s able to locate both the fastball and his plus-flashing slider with mature precision and consistency for a player with his age and frame. There’s a lot of projection ahead here, too, because Hirschkorn is clearly not done filling out, and he has the short, loose arm stroke and feel for pitching that make me bullish he can also develop a pretty good offspeed pitch. Atlanta’s had a lot of success developing high school players on both sides of the ball in recent years, which makes the already-intriguing Hirschkorn a particularly interesting follow in his first pro season.

Name: Allen Facundo
Report:
Injuries, including a 2024 Tommy John, limited Facundo's pro reps from 2022 through 2025. During that span, his fastball velocity ticked up from the 89-92 mph range to the 92-95 mph range, though he was hardly healthy enough to notice. When he returned from elbow rehab in the second half of 2025, Facundo was throwing harder still, scraping 99 and sitting 95 while bending in a slider nasty enough that teams could have considered him a justifiable Rule 5 target as a reliever last offseason. When stretched out to work a career-high 114 innings in 2026, Facundo's velo slipped a tad and he walked a whopping 78 batters, reinforcing a relief projection, but his slider is so good that if his peak fastball velocity returns upon a full-time conversion to the bullpen, he could turn into a high-leverage, low-slot reliever à la José A. Ferrer. 
Facundo's delivery is almost a dead ringer for Ferrer's, essentially a sidearm operation with side-spinning fastballs, changeups, and sliders. This slot bolsters the effectiveness of his slider, which has big length and nasty, late bite. It plays as a plus-plus bat-missing weapon against hitters of either handedness. His other stuff needs polish. Facundo's fastball release is noticeably different than it is for his other pitches, and he doesn't locate it well. His changeup is like a glorified upper-80s sinker; it has utility as a way to induce weak contact, but it's seldom used. Facundo's grade here assumes that an eventual conversion to relief will bring back his peak 2025 fastball velo, which would make him an impact late-inning lefty.

Name: Juan Caricote
Report:
Caricote was Toronto’s top signee in the 2026 international class, an athletic catcher who inked a $1.9 million deal. He’s a good mover with a nice blend of present bat speed and growth ahead. He has a lofted bat path, and when he drops the bat head into the lefty happy zone, he can unleash a ferocious and powerful swing. The mechanics are also fairly low maintenance. He has a little hitch in his load, but he’s direct to the ball from there, he gets the foot down early, and he swings with an appropriate level of effort.
Caricote had a productive DSL debut, hitting .274/.369/.433 with five homers, though with a little more swing and miss than his 16.4% strikeout rate would imply. His approach is immature — he chased 32% of the time, 52% with two strikes — but at this stage, it’s better to ask a guy to pull back on the reins than to turn it loose more often.
Defensively, Caricote looks good. He’s a remarkably smooth receiver for a player his age, and he has a strong arm as well. His release is long and at times a little stiff, and there’s room for growth when it comes to his accuracy, but at his age, that’s normal and expected, as is a tendency to stab too much on balls in the dirt. You don't need him to catch tomorrow, you need him to do so in five years, and the forecast is for him to play well back there when the time comes. There’s enough uncertainty in a player this young and far away from the majors that we're not quite ready to get irresponsible with the topline FV grade. A year in, though, it looks like Toronto gave their big bonus to the right guy. Caricote projects as an everyday catcher.

Name: Kaiden McCarthy
Report:
McCarthy reclassified from the 2027 class and was selected in the second round this past July. He signed with the Braves for $2.5 million, which was somehow the fourth-largest outlay of Atlanta’s monster draft. He dominated overmatched northeast high schoolers all spring, then was electric at the Combine, where he scraped 100. He’s an explosive, if undersized, athlete who not only throws hard, but also has very nasty secondary stuff, including a changeup with ridiculous tailing action.
McCarthy’s velo has come on very quickly. He was sitting 92-94 mph 18 months ago, but touched 101 weeks before the draft. McCarthy tends to live in the 94-98 mph range across whole outings, with rise/tail shape and a flat angle created by his stature. He’s a six foot tall high school righty, a demographic teams are terrified of because its health and development track record isn't great. Every once in a while there’s a Dylan Cease who can maintain this kind of velo and be durable, but it’s more common for a pitcher’s velo to tank when he’s forced to work every week for six months. For now, we can only guess how sustainable all this is in McCarthy’s case. If he can look like this all season, his upside is very high indeed.

Name: Jake Bloss
Report:
It's been a tough couple of years for Bloss. After a brief big league debut with Houston in 2024, he entered 2025 on the cusp of making the Blue Jays rotation, but tore his UCL six starts into the minor league season. Bloss returned to the mound this past summer with his arm strength intact but with very little touch and feel, and he took a beating in four Triple-A starts. He then went back on the shelf in mid-July and was eventually transferred to the 60-day IL with a right teres major strain that cost him the rest of the regular season. He was back throwing for short stretches in the Arizona Fall League, where he sat 93-95. 
Prior to the injury, Bloss looked like a relatively safe mid-rotation starter. He had, and has, a power pitcher's frame and a north-south attack with a bunch of weapons. His mid-90s four-seamer projects plus and is further aided by above-average carry. His upper-80s slider was the big bat-misser before surgery, and his 12-6 hammer of a curve was plenty good as well. His change was hampered a bit by a slower arm path, though he reliably kept it to the arm side, and lefties mostly weren't able to drive it. Periodically, Bloss looked like that guy again in 2026. His average fastball was harder than at last glance, at least during the regular season. He was throwing his breaking balls a little firmer as well, and the curve in particular looked really sharp at times.
But Bloss wasn't fully himself. His release point was inconsistent, he wasn't generating as much extension, he threw a bunch of cement-mixer sliders, and his two-seamer got whacked. Setbacks aren't unusual for a pitcher shaking off cobwebs, though the degree to which Bloss got hit around (10 homers in 39.1 minor league innings across three levels) was a little surprising. I still like him and, health willing, see a path to the mid-rotation projection he had last year. Between the injury and uneven performance, though, he slides into this FV tier for now.

Name: Rory Fox
Report:
Fox was his Waukesha high school's valedictorian and a fourth generation Golden Domer. He moved into the Irish rotation part of the way through his sophomore year and struggled, then improved significantly during his junior season, when he carried a 3.58 ERA during a nutty offensive era for college baseball. The Yankees weren't shy about upping Fox's workload or promotion pace in 2026, his first pro season, as he worked 130 innings (twice what he threw the prior season) and was promoted to Somerset for the final six weeks of the year. 
The velo spike Fox showed at the very end of his junior season carried into 2026, and he sat roughly 93 for the entire year. Three different breaking balls, including a brand new cutter, all create a lot of weak contact. Fox's fastball and slider both generate above-average miss, while his curveball's arm-side bend gives him a way to deal with lefties rather than use his inconsistent changeup. Unless Fox's arm strength keeps climbing, he's going to lack a truly dominant offering, and will instead settle in as a consistent backend option. He's tracking for a mid-to-late-2028 debut.

Name: John Gil
Report:
Gil was a $110,000 signee in the 2023 international period, just enough to graze the radar. He’s been a pleasant surprise since, as plus wheels, solid defense, and a knack for making contact gave him the look of a potential everyday regular up the middle. When he showed up to camp with an extra 10-15 pounds of muscle this past February, I speculated that his newfound size might change that projection, though to this point it mostly hasn’t.
While Gil hit for a little pop in 2026, the jump in homers seems as much a reflection of a carrying minor league baseball as a modest power increase. Gil’s max and 90th-percentile exit velocities went up a little bit, as did his launch angle and whiff rates, but he hasn't changed all that much as a hitter. His bat speed and swing length are about average, and his approach and barrel control remain mature for a 20-year-old. Though not without flaws — he’s often out in front of spin and tends to miss breaking balls low and away — Gil blends a decent hit tool with viable power, particularly given his tendency to pull the ball.
Gil is starting to see a lot of time at second base. Part of that is because Alex Lodise and Tate Southisene are eating into his opportunities, but it’s also a reflection of Gil’s game. He’s a fundamentally sound defender with an above-average arm and tends to handle the routine plays, but despite good straight line speed, he isn't especially rangy yet, and his glovework dips when he has to stretch himself. It’s possible he can still become an average defender at short, but future physical growth is a potential obstacle there.
Ultimately, Gil does a lot well and not much exceptionally. While he still has paths to an everyday role, particularly if either the hit tool or his power exceeds my projection, the winds seem to be blowing toward a utility job. His ability to hit and likely get to at least fringy power makes him a useful player, particularly since it looks like he’s going to have the versatility to play all over the dirt. It’ll be interesting to see if Atlanta experiments with him in the outfield, as his speed gives him the potential to wear a lot of hats.

Name: Gage Stanifer
Report:
Stanifer was arguably Toronto’s 2025 breakout prospect. A late pick out of a suburban Indianapolis high school, he signed for $125,000 and spent two relatively nondescript seasons at the lower levels before turning in a career season in Vancouver. He spent most of 2026 in New Hampshire, where he missed a ton of bats (he struck out more than 30% of hitters) but was also pretty wild (14.5% walk rate).
Stanifer is an above-average athlete with a three-pitch mix. He sits in the mid-90s with a four-seamer that touches the upper 90s. The pitch has carry but also tail and lacks some of the other characteristics that can turn a good fastball into a monster. The pitch tunnels pretty well with his slider, a plus north-south offering that falls off the table and induces some of the best whiff and chase rates in the system. The change is the third offering here, and while he doesn’t execute it consistently, it too flashes plus and actually generated more chase than the slider this past year.
While Stanifer’s delivery isn't violent, it is high-effort. He’s never been a great strike-thrower, and both below-average command and a style of pitching heavily reliant on inducing chase suggest he'll fit better in short stints than the rotation. The Jays don't have to flip that switch just yet; a five-and-dive starting outcome is still in play. But if I were a betting man, I’d stack seven or eight out of 10 chips on a future primarily in relief. Stanifer projects as a nasty, if slightly wild, late-inning reliever.

Name: Chris Kean
Report:
Kean looks like he's going to be a positive example of what an org with a talent for developing pitchers can do with a good athlete who has a nice-looking delivery. Once just a tall, undrafted right-hander with a gorgeous arm action, he now looks likely to be a big leaguer within the next year. 
Kean spent two years at a junior college halfway between Fort Worth and Abilene (the Ranger College Rangers) and then was injured for much of his junior year at Monroe, a season that ended with a Tommy John after just a few innings. Signed as an undrafted free agent in 2023, he dominated when he returned from TJ rehab in 2024, treaded water in 2025, and then developed in two keys ways during a 2026 season in which he had a 5-to-1 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 63 upper minors innings. He improved the demarcation between his breaking balls and added a brand new 90-ish mph splitter/sinker that, depending on which pitch data source team folks are looking at, might not be properly labeled in their sample. This new pitch gives Kean a weapon that finishes in the bottom of the strike zone and below, which he didn't have before. Previously, he would dump both breaking balls into the top of the zone as a way to play off of elevated fastballs, and though this was effective enough — Kean sits 93-94 with nearly pure backspin and generates seven feet of extension; he has real stuff — the added wrinkle has made him less predictable, and more than anything else has aided the bat-missing capacity of his fastball. 
Kean's command and repertoire depth make him a candidate to be stretched out as a long reliever. Were he younger, you could argue for stretching him out even more than that, but because his time on the 40-man looms, there's less opportunity to do so. Likely to be a middle reliever who is good for Yankee fans' blood pressure, Kean is the kind of athlete who might yet throw a bit harder or continue to improve his changeup over time and wind up being the third- or fourth-best arm in a good bullpen.

Name: AJ Gracia
Report:
Atlanta selected Gracia ninth overall this past July, roughly a dozen picks ahead of where we had him on our Board. Going underslot allowed the Braves to sign several interesting high schoolers later in the draft, and they did so while still getting one of the best college bats available.
Gracia is a strapping, broad-shouldered 6-foot-3 center fielder with big league size. He transferred to Virginia for his draft year and hit a career-best .354/.489/.632 with 30 extra-base hits. He has excellent plate coverage and likes to hit the ball to all fields. His selectivity — some might call it passivity — and hand-eye coordination allow him to move the bat around the zone with uncommon feel for such a big, long-levered hitter, and he posted comfortably plus contact rates in his last two college seasons.
Part of the reason this works is that Gracia’s swing is often conservative. He has a small load and then a short, direct cut that doesn't tend to produce much of a follow-through. There’s more verve in the A-swing when he gets it off, but even the biggest of his hacks produced a top-end exit velo of 110 mph. That's nothing to sneeze at on its own, but still pedestrian for a first-round college guy swinging a DeMarini.
The power forecast is especially relevant here because Gracia isn’t a burner. His feel for defense is good, he’s comfortable going back on balls hit over his head, and he looks smooth at the catch point, but he doesn't have the straight-line speed of a typical center fielder, and his arm is well below average. This profile gets tweenerish real fast if his contact ability dips in pro ball, or he loses significant power in the switch to wood.

Name: Danny Thompson Jr.
Report:
Thompson was a $5,000 signee in the 2025 draft, a priority older senior with interesting stuff and release traits but fringy velocity. He’s added nearly two ticks to his fastball since draft day and, combined with a low release and above-average vertical, the pitch has been a real bat-misser. It’s difficult to tell on video if Thompson is working with one breaking ball or two, though the velocity gap is large enough that I’ll guess two. Both are horizontal breakers, one low-80s and one mid-80s with corresponding differences in length. I like the slower, longer one more, as it’s still sharp enough to run off the barrel, while the slider plays like a soft cutter. He’s also got a changeup with late hop to it, though he hasn't thrown it a ton.
Thompson has a chance to start. While he’s not playing catch out there, it’s a clean, up-tempo delivery, and he repeats it well. His command is a little below average now, but he’s good at elevating the fastball, and he isn't so erratic that you'd think that he couldn't improve his location elsewhere, too. The bigger question is endurance. Thompson isn't a big guy, and his velo tends to drop midway through outings. Given that the stuff is more good than great and that the arsenal is pretty shallow, I feel more comfortable projecting him as a backend starter or good multi-inning arm than as a mid-rotation guy. A no. 4 outcome is the ceiling if these concerns prove overblown, or if I’m underrating how well his sneaky fastball will play at the highest level.

Name: Brendan Brock
Report:
Brock is an uncommonly toolsy catching prospect who was initially drafted by the Brewers in 2025 out of Southwestern Illinois Community College but chose to honor his commitment to Oklahoma. That paid off in multiple ways, as his draft stock leapt into the third round and he won a national championship with the Sooners in 2026.  
Brock is still pretty crude in most facets of the game, but he presents New York's player development apparatus with rare physical traits for a catching prospect, including plus-plus speed. He frames pretty well for someone who only has one year of experience catching big conference pitching (Brock successfully framed 60% of pitches in the shadow zone for strikes in 2026, per Synergy), and has a roughly average arm on pure strength. He needs to shorten his exchange and improve his accuracy, and he'll probably have learn how to block pro-quality breaking balls, which he's caught very few of. 
Brock also K'd at a 25.5% clip in 2026, which is a lot for a college hitter. His hands take a bit too long to fire and he inside-outs fastballs to right field, but he's twitchy and might just be a swing tweak away from being on time to pull more often. It's weird to call the national champion's starting backstop a sleeper dev project, but that's what Brock is, and he has a relatively wide range of potential career outcomes, with a puncher's chance to be an everyday catcher.

Name: Brett Sears
Report:
Once a system or so, I encounter a player who makes me go, “And just what the hell am I supposed to do with this?” Sears is that guy in Atlanta. This past year, the righty sat either side of 90, dialed up a fastball about 60% of the time, attacked the zone, and more or less reduced upper-level hitters to tears. Even accounting for good extension, a low release height, and a little more velocity this year than last, the pitch was surprisingly dominant (35.5% CSW) in a way that fastballs in his velo band very rarely are. He executes his other pitches well — a shapely 1-7 curve, a two-plane slider, and an occasional sinking change — but this isn't a case where hitters are too worried about buckling secondaries to sit on the ol’ number one; great deception and plus command have simply worked their magic here. Across 21 starts and 124.1 upper-level innings — quite a few for a starter in this day and age — Sears notched a 2.90 ERA with a 24.9% K-BB%. It’s impressive.
Whether he can do this against better hitters is the looming question. There are a handful of big league starters who operate in this velo band, and while the good ones tend to either have plus-plus breaking balls or throw left-handed, it’s possible that Sears executes well enough to make this work. The topline grade here tries to thread the needle, acknowledging that the additional arm strength and command gains he’s made have materially elevated his ceiling, while also retaining some skepticism about his ability to befuddle the best hitters in the world with smoke and mirrors. If nothing else, Sears is a fascinating player to follow in 2027.

Name: Daniel Guerra
Report:
An Honorable Mention on last year’s list, I profiled Guerra as an arm strength flier who needed to find a breaking ball. A year on, consider one found. The righty added a couple ticks and a little more break to his slider year over year, and the pitch generated a CSW% above 40% in 2026. He doesn't always finish it, and it’s vulnerable in the zone if he hangs one, but when he snaps off a good one that dives late beneath the zone, it’s nigh unhittable. 
Guerra has retained the arm strength that first made him interesting, as he sits in the mid-to-upper 90s and touches triple digits. He also has a change that flashes above average, though it’s even less consistent than his slider. Though he’s started for most of his career, Guerra made a handful of upper level appearances in relief down the stretch, and he projects to stay in that role long-term. He’s an open strider with huge spinal tilt, a big head dip, and noticeable arm slot variation between his fastball and secondaries, the change especially. All of that limits his deception and control, which makes him reliant on out-stuffing hitters. I think he'll be able to do so, and he has late-inning upside if he softens some of the rough edges on his command and execution.

Name: Brendan Beck
Report:
Beck was an ultra-efficient starter at Stanford who signed for just over $1 million as a second-rounder in 2021. Elbow surgeries cost him all of 2022 and 2024, but he has now had two consecutive years with at least 130 innings pitched. What's more, he had a sub-3.00 ERA at Triple-A in 2026 and made his big league debut. 
Beck developed a good splitter in 2026 and now has multiple ways to deal with hitters of either handedness. He can throw his breaking pitches (his best weapons since college) for strikes in any count, which helps him fish for chases with elevated fastballs way above the zone where that slower pitch can avoid danger. The splitter gives Beck a weapon that moves less predictably than his other stuff, and prevents hitters from confidently diving to cover his various breaking balls. He will probably cede a good number of homers just because he sits 92 and pitches in Yankee Stadium, but not so many that he's unrosterable. Beck would be a lot of teams' reliable fifth starter, but because he still has two option years left and is less talented than a totally healthy Yankees rotation, he'll likely graduate as a spot starter in 2027.

Name: Edelson Cabral
Report: Cabral was something of a late bloomer in the 2026 international class and was arguably Atlanta’s best prospect even though others signed for more money. He played a good chunk of the season as a 16-year-old, which adds helpful context to his good-but-not-great production (.236/.397/.344 line, 100 wRC+, 70% contact rate). In the long run, Cabral has a nice swing and should make plenty of contact. He has a shot to develop average power and, as a plus runner with a plus arm, he looks like a good bet to stick at shortstop. With a well-rounded skill set, Cabral has everyday upside and a few paths to add value in a utility role if the bat isn't quite potent enough for regular duty.

Name: Blaine Bullard
Report:
Bullard’s strong commitment to Texas A&M pushed him out of the top rounds of the 2025 draft where his talent belonged. Toronto plucked him in the 12th and signed him for just shy of $1.7 million, the largest bonus ever given to a player selected so late in the draft. 
At the time, the wiry Texan had the look of a slash-and-dash speedster, but Bullard flashed a little more power and a fair bit less contact than expected at Low-A in 2026. Part of that is because lefties crushed him (34 strikeouts in 85 plate appearances) in a way that suggests he might not be a switch-hitter for long. As a lefty, he takes a good rip and has decent plate coverage with less than two strikes; with two strikes, his no-load cut looks unnatural and did nothing to prevent him from chasing significantly more often than he did earlier in counts. There are kinks to work out here, but with his athleticism and at least a little juice, you can see enough bat coming to let the glove play its way onto a roster. 
Defensively, Bullard is fast enough for the job in center. His routes and footwork look pretty good on tape, at least, and he could be plus there at maturity. It’s the overall skill set of a modern day fourth outfielder.

Name: Cade Smith
Report:
Smith is a breaking ball merchant with below-average velocity who had the healthiest and most durable season of his career in 2026 (124.2 innings, 30 more than his previous single-season high), but also carried a bloated 5.27 ERA because he gave up homers on 19% of his fly balls. A lack of velocity (Smith sits about 91) and a tendency to live in the meat of the strike zone have long made this a possibility, but it wasn't actually reflected in Smith's results until he reached Double-A. He was especially homer-prone during the start of the season, and then walk-prone late, perhaps as he tried not to give up so many dingers. Though he has never had microscopic walk rates, Smith has a very fluid and athletic delivery, and doesn't struggle to throw strikes. 
The ability to alter the shape of three different quality balls — an oft-used, strike-getting gyro slider, plus chaseable sweepers and curveballs deployed depending on the hitter's handedness — and use them in any count is what gives Smith a stable starter's projection. If it turns out his fastball is going to get crushed (it yielded a .415 xwOBA in 2026, and his breaking ball usage was way, way up across the board compared to 2025), then he's maybe just a no. 6 or 7 starter. But Smith's delivery, athleticism, and feel for spin are all things that might allow for effective tinkering throughout his career. This grade is reflective of a true no. 5 starter who gives you 130-ish acceptable innings every year.

Name: Alex Lodise
Report:
Lodise signed for seven figures, the third-highest bonus in the Braves’ spread-the-cash-around approach to the top of the 2025 draft. He had an odd debut season. The Braves tend to challenge their prospects, but even though Lodise was a high pick who starred at a major college program, he spent most of the season in Low-A. He hit well and earned a promotion to Double-A by year’s end and he actually performed better there than he did in Augusta.
The big change to Lodise’s offensive report is a drop in his power grade. His 90th-percentile and max EVs (104.6 and 109.8 mph, respectively) were fringy and significantly lower than his marks at Florida State. That’s still decent power, particularly for a shortstop, but combined with some swing-and-miss to his game, his offensive ceiling looks a tad lower this year than it did on draft day. Lodise has a grooved swing that often leaves him behind on fastballs upstairs, and he’s also vulnerable to spin, both at the front door and low and away off the plate. Taken together, he can drive a pitch in the lower third of the plate, but there are otherwise a lot of places to get him out.
Defensively, Lodise is a no-doubt shortstop. He moves well in all directions, his hands are fast, and he has a strong and accurate hose. He isn't perfect; he’ll sometimes kick a ball when he has to hurry, but he’s a good defensive shortstop, and he’s played well at second in the few chances he’s had at that position as well. Guys with good gloves up the middle and a little thump tend to play for a while even with a shaky hit tool. Lodise projects as a quality utility infielder, with an upside resembling Paul DeJong’s if he can find a way to make enough contact.

Name: Core Jackson
Report:
Jackson, who grew up in Ontario, was understandably off some teams' draft boards during the 2023 to 2025 window in which he was eligible because of an incident where he drew a swastika on the dorm room door of a Jewish student while he was a freshman at Nebraska and then an impaired driving charge at Utah a couple of years later. The Yankees took him in the 2025 fifth round.
Graded purely on talent here, Jackson projects to be a glove-first utility infielder thanks to his acrobatic body control, plus hands, and arm strength. He has now had pro exposure to all the infield positions besides first base, and he's meaningfully good at all three. He had a great regular season as a hitter, as he posted a .259/.369/.474 line at Hudson Valley and then a 100 wRC+ at Somerset during the final month of the year. Jackson also has some interesting underlying metrics, including a 49% hard-hit rate and a 106 mph EV90.
If we were basing his offensive evaluation purely on the data, we might conclude that Jackson projects as an everyday shortstop, as both his contact and power numbers hovered around the big league average, which would be great for the position. But Jackson's swing takes a fairly long time to enter the hitting zone, and he can get tied up around his hands. After three IL stints during the regular season (hamstring strain, concussion, thigh strain) limited his playing time, he struggled in the Arizona Fall League badly enough that it became tough to take his regular season stats at face value. Jackson will likely spend 2027 in Somerset and could end up in the majors if enough injuries befall the big league roster. On his own timeline, though, he's likely to debut late in 2028.

Name: Jhon Rivas
Report: Rivas was a small-dollar international signee in the 2025 class. He’s athletic with a live arm, and while his fastball isn't optimized, he peppers in plenty of 95s and 96s. He also has a wipeout slider that flashes plus; DSL complex hitters were completely overwhelmed by it when it was anywhere near the strike zone. While that’s a great foundation for a pitching prospect, the road ahead is long and arduous. Rivas doesn't yet have a changeup, and he’s a short, high-effort pitcher and thus even more of an injury risk than your average teenager with his kind of gas. Various teams will handle the upside/proximity dilemma a little differently with a guy like this. We're putting a 40 FV on Rivas for now, but that could change quickly if he either develops a viable change or scampers off the complex in 2027.

Name: Garrett Baumann
Report:
Baumann’s last two seasons are a tale of two steps forward and one step back. After a velo uptick and an intriguing splitter propelled the Florida native to a big season at High-A in 2025, upper-level hitters proved a sterner test in 2026, and his initial exposure to Triple-A in particular was pretty ugly. He lost a tick of velocity, hitters torched his breaking balls, and while he got more consistent with his split, it’s starting to look like more of a 55 pitch than the plus offering I projected in March.
There are still things to like here. Baumann has excellent body control and repeats his delivery well. He has advanced fastball command for a pitcher his age, much less one his size, and that applies to both his four-seamer and sinker. In theory, Baumann’s plus extension and unusually high release point should provide hitters with a tricky angle from which to pick up the ball. In other ways, though, he isn't especially deceptive, as his motion is fairly easy to time and he doesn't seem to hide the ball well. This feels especially true with his breaking stuff, which looks fringy to average to my eye, but got hit around like a meatball statistically.
Baumann finished his season with three decent, if unspectacular, Triple-A starts. Despite the rough ride overall, I remain optimistic that he can start. He throws strikes, generates grounders with his sinker, misses bats with the split, and has the underlying ingredients to spin a couple of useful breaking balls. Baumann still projects as a backend starter, though a middle or multi-inning relief fallback looks a tad more likely than it did 12 months ago.

Name: Wilberson De Pena
Report:
De Pena is a toolsy young outfield prospect. He had a power breakout in his second DSL season but was still often buried toward the bottom of the Angels' lineup down there, and he was hitting seventh the day he was traded to the Yankees for Oswald Peraza in 2025. The Yankees assigned him to the Florida Complex League to start 2026 and there De Pena went nuclear, with an OPS well over 1.000 and 16 homers in 56 games. By the end of the summer, which included a promotion and a nearly month-long stint on the Low-A Tampa roster, he had netted a 20/20 season. The promotion exposed De Pena's lack of breaking ball recognition, however, as he chased and missed them in excess (he had a 46% contact rate against sliders) as a Tarpon. 
If Richard Matic was the linebacker of the complex roster, De Pena was the running back. He's muscular and cut, explosive and fast, and he swings really hard. He has above-average raw power as a 20-year-old, and it will likely be a bit better than that at maturity. De Pena's problem is that he's so hell bent on pulling everything that he swings inside a ton of breaking balls, including ones that finish on the plate. His contact rate tumbled from 72% in the 2025 DSL to 68% in the 2026 FCL, then 63% in the FSL, a troubling trend that indicates he might strike out 30% of the time or more at the higher levels. Still a power/speed threat who runs well enough to continue developing in center field, De Pena's projection is akin to Jacoby Jones or a toolsier Stuart Fairchild.

Name: Victor Arias
Report:
Arias was a Pick to Click for me this spring; that we're just now getting to him tells you that he did not, in fact, vault into our Top 100. Shoulder surgery on his non-throwing arm delayed the start of his season and he never really got going at the plate. He finished the campaign with a .220/.278/.367 line, just a 70 wRC+ and no improvement to the concerning, though not quite disqualifying, walk and strikeout totals he posted in 2025. He has the tools and just enough contact skill to think a breakout is still possible, but his projection is down year over year.
Let’s start with the good. Arias is an athletic, short-levered lefty with above-average present raw power. He has a fast bat, and he’s able to generate that pop without sky-high swing-and-miss or particularly concerning chase data. Even in a down year, his hard-hit rate (44%) was among the highest in the system, and his max exit velocity (113 mph) was fourth in the entire organization, big leaguers included.
The trouble is that all that thump isn't translating into doubles and homers. It’s possible that the way Arias swings doesn't give him enough barrel control to leverage his power. He doesn't get cheated at the plate: He takes a big leg kick, loads deep, and lets it fly with everything he has. It’s a high-effort cut, and it comes with an early front side leak that limits his ability to cover the plate. And while he’s able to deliver the barrel to all quadrants, he hasn't found a way to elevate the ball consistently yet. Last year in this space I wrote, “Might there be a tradeoff to make here? Arias’ max exit velos are comfortably plus. If a smaller move or more controlled swing facilitates more contact at the expense of a little juice, the swap could be worth its weight in gold.” I still think it’s a possibility, and with it, a path to an everyday role.
Defensively, the tape looks better year over year. Arias is still a plus runner and he does a lot of good stuff in center. He plays hard, takes a good route, isn't afraid of the wall, and has a pretty good arm. With even a little more game pop, he has the foundation of a solid fourth outfielder.

Name: Jose Manon
Report: Manon stood out for his bat speed and physical projection as an amateur. A high-effort swing made him something of a risky bet from a hit tool perspective, but so far, so good.
