Additional strength helped Manon keep his swing under control, and neither his strikeout totals nor swing-and-miss data looked particularly scary in his first DSL exposure. The 17-year-old already has fringy pop and a chance to grow into quite a bit more. There could be some push and pull as he matures, as Manon is on the third base/shortstop line and has a bigger frame than most guys who stay up the middle. His plus arm would play well at the hot corner if he has to move, though, and a left-side defender with this kind of power projection is an interesting follow regardless of where he winds up.

Name: Mac Heuer
Report:
Add Heuer to the list of pitchers who have gotten better after they've left Texas Tech. Homeschooled in Georgia for high school, Heuer was a draft-eligible sophomore in 2025 who was operating with low-in-the-zone fastballs and well-located secondary pitches. WIthin a year of signing, his conditioning improved, the pace and intensity of Heuer's delivery ratcheted up, and he was working with elevated, naturally-cutting fastballs that were suddenly touching 98. In addition to his cutting four-seamer, the Yankees had him working with three other breaking balls in 2026 (slider, sweeper, curveball) and scrapped his changeup. Walk and strikeouts were the theme of five healthy starts with Tampa, but Heuer suffered an elbow sprain in early June and was shut down for the rest of the year.
Realistically, Heuer will be a power reliever who ends up with just one or two of the breaking balls he worked with in 2026. He isn't a great athlete and his delivery requires a ton of effort for him to throw hard, but he can really spin it, and he might sustain upper-90s heat if he's working a single inning at a time. This is a high-variance arm who you could argue belongs next to Allen Facundo in the 40+ FV tier as a potential late-inning reliever, but the injury and command questions surrounding Heuer prevent such stuffage this go 'round.

Name: Juan Sanchez
Report:
Sanchez was one of Toronto’s big-dollar signees in the 2025 international class. He had a strong debut campaign in the DSL and parlayed that and a hot spring into a surprise assignment to Low-A Dunedin. The youngest regular in the league, Sanchez often looked out of his depth on both sides of the ball. After initially treading water, he struggled down the stretch and finished the season with a 70 wRC+. Combined with worrying data under the hood and a rough performance at third base, Sanchez will almost certainly need to repeat the level in 2027. 
The bat, and the projectable power more specifically, is Sanchez’s calling card. His 103 mph EV90 and 108 max exit velo are both great for a guy who played the season as an 18-year-old, and he has sufficient projection left on his frame to think that plus raw at maturity is a real possibility. That pop didn't make its way into games much, though, in part because he’s so expansive (his chase rate was nearly 40% and jumped to nearly 50% with two strikes) and is constantly flailing at spin in particular. He’s also prone to missing fastballs up, as his swing path is grooved and he isn't consistently able to get the bat head to the top of the zone. More bat speed will help, and Sanchez is likely to grow into plenty. Overall though, he looks more like a potential power threat than a well-rounded offensive force. 
Sanchez had a rough defensive campaign as well, as the game often looked too fast for him on that side of the ball. Fielding percentage isn't relevant unless it starts with an eight, which Sanchez’s did. He booted all manner of balls — short hops to the backhand were particularly vexing — and while he has the arm strength for third, he'll need to clean up the scatter on his throws to stay there. While he has time to work himself into an average defender at the hot corner, I think it’s unlikely, and a shift to left field or first base looms as a real possibility. The Jays and their fans can hope that Sanchez’s difficult 2026 season is attributable be attributed mostly to age. At the very least, it’s time to take him off the fast track.

Name: Carter Beck
Report:
The Braves got the 26th pick in the 2026 draft as a reward for rostering 2025 Rookie of the Year winner Drake Baldwin all season long. They used that selection to take Beck, a toolsy Canadian outfielder with a small-school college background, and sign him for $2.6 million. The gap between Beck’s place on our Draft Board (a third- or fourth-round flier in the unranked section of our college hitters) and where he ultimately went was large enough that we immediately flagged him as a guy for a thorough review at season’s end. Fortunately, Beck signed quickly and was able to play in 29 total games across the A-ball affiliates. These late-season cameos are often tricky places to evaluate a guy, but given his background, it’s fair to place a little more weight on how Beck looked in pro ball than I’d otherwise be inclined to do.
And Beck performed pretty well. He notched a 123 wRC+ with a couple of homers, a 17.8% strikeout rate, and a 16.3% walk rate. Visually, he has a funky swing, which makes for an odd look. He’s an open strider with an early hip leak and a flat, at times downhill, bat path. He’s able to drive pitches when he gets the bat head out front early — his average launch angle was 11 degrees in pro ball, which is just fine — but he does hit a fair number of groundballs. He’s short-levered and quick to the ball, and he likes to get his arms extended; most of his hardest and most productive contact came on pitches up and away from him. None of the swing or contact data under the hood stood out. His swing and contact rates were pretty normal for a prospect. He chased a fair bit with two strikes and often looked unbalanced against good changeups, neither of which is abnormal for a guy who hasn't seen much good pitching.
Defensively, Beck’s tape in center is okay. He’s an above-average runner, which is enough for the middle pasture, though you’d ideally like someone faster. He made a few nice reads on liners to his left and right and had a few moments he’d like back on flies over his head, but you can squint and see an average defender up the middle. Size and future growth loom as potential hurdles, as Beck is well-built already and presumably won't get swifter; it’s possible he has a peak as a viable center fielder, but needs to shift to a corner relatively early in his career.
Ultimately, Beck doesn't have glaring weaknesses and has a nice blend of power and functional bat-to-ball skills for an up-the-middle player. There’s not an obvious carrying tool here, though, and so while he has the ceiling of an everyday outfielder, any of the yellow flags — potential inability to get to launch, vulnerability against soft stuff, speed degradation — threaten to turn this into a fourth outfielder’s profile in short order.

Name: Kyle Carr
Report: Carr left San Diego after what scout sources indicate to be "attendance issues" at USD. He certainly found a new gear on the field at Palomar, where, toward the end of the 2023 season, he was touching 97 mph and holding 93-95 deep into starts. Carr hasn't maintained that velocity in pro ball and only averaged 91-92 mph in 2026, but he can reliably throw his four-seamer and cutter (most used against righties) for strikes, and attack lefties with a sinker and slider. Carr will subtly manipulate the shape of his breaking balls and throw some eephus-style low-70s curves. He's unlikely to be an impact arm, but he should be a reliable swingman and bulk reliever.

Name: Chad Dallas
Report:
Dallas, a.k.a. Cheese, returned from Tommy John surgery no worse for wear. Out since mid-2024, he made a handful of starts for Buffalo before getting summoned to the big leagues for a few multi-inning outings. He was a little wild there, but missed bats with his breaking balls. Dallas spins the ball well, and he leans on his breakers: His best pitch is an above-average sweeper, and he’s also got a more traditional 12-6 hook that he likes to steal strikes with. While he has a sinker, he doesn't use it a ton and relies instead on a low-90s cutter when he wants something firm and (relatively) straight.
Dallas is a perfect fit for our “MIRP” tag. He has the graceful delivery and, in turn, control of a starter, and his stuff is good enough that he doesn't need to air everything out for 15-20 pitches to be effective. It’s not an attack likely to survive multiple trips through a big league lineup, though, as Dallas needs to induce chase on breaking balls that are sharp but not especially firm. Working as a starter in the minors, he’s been dinger-prone throughout his career, and it looks like his best path to value is as a one to three inning guy who can spot start (if anybody still bothers with that in this era). He’s poised to contribute regularly in low-to-mid-leverage work in 2027.

Name: Owen Carey
Report:
Carey was a 15th-rounder in 2024 who signed for a modest bonus out of high school, an increasingly rare player demographic. He quickly emerged as an intriguing outfield prospect, a do-a-little-bit-of-everything type and a sleeper in this system for both scouts and analysts. Just 20, he’s already reached Double-A, and while he didn't hit much at Columbus this past summer, both his hit tool and defensive versatility are promising. 
Carey has a pretty lefty swing with a late loft. While his bat isn't fast, it isn't slow either, and there’s real venom in his A-swing. As is the case for a lot of young players, good spin has been a problem, but it was his performance against the fastball at Double-A that explains the big spike in his K% and swing-and-miss rate. He doesn't flatten the bat much on pitches upstairs, and he had trouble getting his hands high enough to hit heaters up in the zone. He'll have to find a way to do so, and given his previous performance and general hitterish profile, I suspect he will. 
On last cycle's list, I speculated that Carey wasn't likely to grow into a ton of power, and so far that’s held. If he gained any raw thump, it didn't show up in the data — his 90th-percentile and max EVs were a tick lower, actually — and there’s a chance that he’s just not going to grow into a whole lot more physicality. His defensive responsibilities have also narrowed. Though he looked fine while playing all three outfield spots in 2025 and made several highlight-reel grabs in right this year, Carey didn't see any time in center. I don't think it’s out of the question that he could play up the middle, but it doesn't seem to be part of Atlanta’s plan for him. Taken together, Carey still looks like a fourth outfielder prospect, but he’s running out of paths to exceed that forecast.

Name: Thatcher Hurd
Report:
Hurd was a famous high school prospect with a great breaking ball, and was a candidate to go toward the back of the 2021 first round. Instead, he ended up at UCLA for a year before he became one of several high-profile players to transfer to LSU in 2023. The team was so good during his time there that Hurd never got his footing in the Tigers rotation, moving into a swingman role as a junior after two bad starts in early 2024. He posted a 1.06 ERA at UCLA, but he struggled with walks and had an ERA closer to 6.00 in Baton Rouge. Hurd blew out during his first spring training and didn't pitch at an affiliate until May of 2026. By July, he had finally stretched out to five innings a couple of times, but he promptly got hurt again (elbow inflammation) and missed the second half of the season. 
Hurd's curveball is awesome, an old school 12-to-6 yakker with special spin and depth, but his fastball isn't good, struggling to miss bats because it has hittable downhill angle. An upper-80s cutter will likely become his primary early-count pitch as Hurd climbs the minor league ladder, and it's fair to assume he'll end up with a slower, lateral-moving breaker that could also be plus because of his talent for spinning the baseball. Hurd basically hasn't been an effective starter since 2022, and might be limited to a relief role because of his fastball's lack of playability.

Name: Ryan Sprock
Report:
Sprock signed for $225,000 out of Elon, a small Division I school. He played both corner infield positions there and was pretty good on the mound, too, where he touched 96 mph in relief. Though he never caught in college, the Twins started working him in behind the plate shortly after the draft, and he took to the position well. He split his time between catcher and third base across two levels for Minnesota before the Blue Jays acquired him in July in the Tommy Nance trade.
The experiment behind the plate is off to a good start, though Sprock isn't a finished product back there. He’s a surprisingly clean receiver for someone so new to the job, and he’s good at funneling balls back toward the center of the plate. He tends to flinch as he does it, so there’s some push and pull to his framing work in the here and now. His catch-and-throw skills are raw: He has plenty of arm strength, but he isn't quick out of the crouch, and his throws are pretty scattered. As with his receiving, there are times when he lines everything up mechanically and the operation looks big league-caliber. As you’d expect, though, he needs a lot of reps to build consistency. He’s athletic and still new to this, and forecasting him as an average defender feels aggressive but realistic.
The Jays will presumably be patient with him there because the bat isn't all that likely to profile by itself. He’s part of Toronto’s brigade of 30- or 40-power prospects who can hit. Sprock's contact rate was nearly 85%, 88% in zone, and his short and punchy swing should continue to allow him to make plenty of contact as he reaches the upper levels. He projects as a utility player with a unique flavor, with a little upside if he really takes to the job behind the plate.

Name: Davis Polo
Report: Polo pitched well in his return to the mound from Tommy John surgery. In 2026, he started 18 times and threw 99.2 innings of 3.25 ERA ball with good peripherals at Low-A, then made a handful of appearances all the way up the chain in the season’s final weeks. Polo is a smooth operator with a clean delivery and a loose arm swing. He has a starter’s control and mechanics, but is unusually reliant on his slider for a length arm. It’s a good pitch with above-average snap and late depth, and he commands it well. He also missed a ton of bats with his change, which plays up due to his ability to locate. A light fastball limits the grade here, as Polo sits in the low 90s without bat-missing shape. He projects as a backend starter and could also be a very good version of the one-time-through guys we saw a fair bit of this past October. The Braves added him to their 40-man roster just prior to publication.

Name: Tyler Boudreau
Report:
A Canadian high schooler, Boudreau was a dominant starter at Midland College in Texas for two of his three seasons there before transferring to Texas Tech, where he struggled as the Red Raider's Saturday night guy for much of 2025. Signed as an undrafted free agent, he was deployed as a starter at Low-A Tampa for much of 2026 and pitched well — 106.2 innings, 27.6% strikeout rate, 9.4% walk rate, 3.29 ERA on the year — with an overhauled delivery. 
The Yankees have raised Boudreau's arm slot a good bit, and  his heater now has nearly perfect backspinning ride and averages just over 19 inches of vertical movement. The new arm slot also allows Boudreau to get on top of his breaking ball better. He's athletic and has a clean-looking, repeatable delivery, as well as a tailing changeup that garnered a slightly above-average rate of whiffs in 2026 and has projection because his arm action is so nice. Obviously, Boudreau's performance should be taken with a healthy grain of salt because he was an older guy pitching in the Florida State League, but there's interesting raw material here that the Yankees have helped make better already, so it's plausible he's in line for a 2027 breakout.

Name: Franklin Rojas
Report:
Rojas signed for just shy of $1 million in the 2024 international class. After two solid statistical seasons in the DSL, he just about Xeroxed that production in the FCL, where he hit .266/.413/.427 with nearly as many walks as strikeouts. That's in line with the competitive, if not special, production we've forecast for him since he signed. He's a patient hitter with a fairly short swing and good bat-to-ball skills. He isn't especially projectable and he wasn't in great shape, but he should have enough pop to chip a few balls over the fence at maturity. 
If Rojas makes it, the glove will be a big part of why. He's a quiet receiver with a good arm and the physicality we like to see in a catcher. He's sometimes content to try to stab at balls in the dirt rather than get in front of them, but he has time on his side to improve as a blocker. He has everyday upside if either his pop or defensive grade exceeds this projection.

Name: Patrick Clohisy
Report:
Clohisy quietly had a breakout 2026 season, hitting .290/.372/.457 (122 wRC+) across 112 games split between Columbus and Gwinnett. The 24-year-old has been a pleasant surprise since he was drafted in 2024, when he signed for the standard $150,000 bonus players picked in the 11th round or later receive. He’s ascended through Atlanta’s system quickly and has developed relevant power to go along with plus wheels and good instincts on the bases and in center.
Clohisy hits from a slightly closed stance. He doesn't have a particularly quick bat, and his feel for contact is more okay than great. He isn't especially vulnerable to any one pitch or location, though, and he’s shown the capacity to make adjustments mid-at-bat, which strengthens my conviction he'll put the ball in play often enough to have a career. Provided he does, everything else gets pretty exciting. Unlike a lot of speedsters in center, he has enough pop to chip in a few dingers, and once he’s on the bases, he’s a threat to run at any time. Clohisy stole 100 bags in 2025 (if you count his AFL tally) and swiped another 62 at the upper levels in 2026. Defensively, he’s a plus center fielder who gets good jumps and can make highlight-reel catches at the edge of his range. He’s a fun watch, and while I don't see quite enough stick here for regular duty, Clohisy stands a decent chance of turning into a fan-favorite fourth outfield type.

Name: Tony Rossi
Report:
Rossi spent time at Division-II West Florida and a junior college before he ended up at Charlotte for three years, one of which he missed due to elbow surgery. He entered pro ball in 2025 at age 25 and had a great (if fairly walk-prone) first season as he posted a 2.18 ERA and struck out 33.7% of opponents. In 2026, he cut his walks down to 6.6% while maintaining his K%, including after he was promoted to Double-A Somerset in early June. Perhaps more importantly, Rossi's fastball velocity was a bit more consistent than the year before, as he sat 94-96 pretty much all season, and continued to do so with Culiacan in the Mexican Winter League. 
Rossi throws pretty hard and has a great sweeper. Even as we're cautious about over-assigning the "sweeper" label to breaking balls, Rossi's definitely is one, as it features 14 inches of horizontal break on average. It was an utterly dominant pitch for him in college and generated a 52% miss rate each of the last two years, which is an elite mark. The combination of a fastball that lacks effective movement and a pedestrian changeup, which Rossi emphasized against lefties in 2026, is likely to create a notable platoon split in the majors. Especially if some of his strike-throwing improvement sticks, Rossi looks like a rock solid middle reliever, if a bit of a righty specialist.

Name: Brandon Barriera
Report: A first-rounder back in 2022, Barriera’s career has since been defined by injuries, and the 38.2 frames he threw in 2026 were a career high. Understandably, he was rusty, with a lot of walks and less velo than he showed at his peak. While Barriera mixed in a few cutters and changeups, he mostly worked with his fastball and slider this past season. He dropped his slot slightly year over year, and now gets a little more run on his low-to-mid-80s slide piece. That pitch flashes plus, and he’s touched the upper 90s with his heater in the past. That would be a suitable mix all by itself in short stints, and given how much time he’s missed with injury, it’s sensible to project a relief outcome here. On stuff, there’s enough to dream on him developing into a good club’s first lefty out of the ‘pen.

Name: Ethan Bagwell
Report:
Bagwell turned in a solid sophomore season. Sent back to Low-A to start the campaign, he quickly breezed through Augusta and posted a 3.83 ERA with good peripherals (8.10/2.25/1.13 pitcher slash) in eight starts after a promotion to Rome. He looks better and stronger year over year. He cleaned up some of the low-hanging fruit in his delivery, most notably by improving his front leg deceleration, and he’s now throwing a tick or two harder than he did in 2025. His changeup took a step forward, which gives him two pitches that flash plus, and his control is already quite good for a player his age.
Still, even with a velo bump, below-average arm strength limits my enthusiasm here. Bagwell's ability to throw quality strikes from a low slot, add and subtract with his breaking ball, and locate a couple of mature secondaries will help him plow through the low and mid-minors, and there’s a chance his feel for location is good enough to exceed my topline forecast. I tend to think he’s more of a backend arm, though, and unless the Braves have a way to extract even more arm strength from his relatively mature frame, I don't see a ton of obvious paths to more than that. He’s graded here as a high-floor/low-ceiling future big league arm.

Name: Wilmy Sanchez
Report: Acquired from Houston at the very start of the 2026 minor league season, Sanchez is an powerfully-built 5-foot-9 reliever who creates such tension via the separation of his hips and shoulders that he's touched 97-98 each of the last few years. He peppers the top of the strike zone with a riding mid-90s fastball and two different breaking balls, but what really emerged for Wilmy after the trade was a tailing changeup that at times has plus-plus action. He K'd 14 per 9 IP at Hudson Valley. Sanchez's approach to pitching is already inefficient as he tries to live around the very top of the strike zone with his fastball/breaking ball combo, but he also lacks feel for release and throws a lot of non-competitive pitches. Though he's more of an explosive athlete than a coordinated one, WIlmy is young enough to project that his command will develop enough to make him a viable middle reliever. His changeup hs a chance to be a special pitch.

Name: John Klein
Report: Klein is an undrafted success story who rose from Iowa Central Community College to the majors after adding bulk and velocity to his big, broad 6-foot-5 frame. He now boasts a rise-and-run heater that touches 97 mph, but more often sits lower, particularly as he gets deeper into outings. Klein has primarily worked as a starter throughout his career, but I'm skeptical his secondaries are good enough to turn a lineup over multiple times. In short stints, the fastball might play as a plus pitch, and if his breaking balls get any sharper alongside, he could have a couple of average complementary weapons to keep hitters honest. He debuted this past season and looks like a near-ready middle reliever.

Name: Tyler Uberstine
Report:
Uberstine was a late bloomer in college and an unheralded 19th-rounder out of Northwestern. He had to prove himself at each minor league level, and after a strong campaign at Triple-A in 2025 (3.56 ERA, 10.09 SO/9, 3.66 BB/9 in about five innings per outing), he briefly debuted with the Red Sox in long relief this April. That switch to the bullpen seems to be permanent, as he continued to work in a relief role in Atlanta’s system after he was dealt to the Braves at the deadline.
Uberstine’s mechanics are clean and repeatable. He works on the first base side of the rubber, strides nearly straight down the mound, lands cleanly, and throws with moderate-to-high effort while staying under control. He hides the ball well, and that and a short stroke give him enough deception to help a deep, if vanilla, mix play ahead of the sum of its parts. He doesn’t lean on any one offering. Uberstine can touch 97 but lives 91-94 with his fastballs and often pitches backwards. The slider/cutter (it looks like the former, but tends to be classified as the latter) and change are sharper, in the upper 80s, and play well together but aren't big swing-and-miss pitches on their own. His slow sweeper is a timing disruptor. 
Now 27, Uberstine looks just about ready to go. He pitched well in a multi-inning relief role in Triple-A — 28.7% K rate, 8.7% walk rate, 3.20 ERA across 56.1 innings — and projects to do something similar when he gets an extended crack in the majors.

Name: Jay Harry
Report:
Harry’s 2026 breakout was one of the farm’s most unexpected developments. A year after his aggressive and relatively punchless approach was thoroughly exploited by mid-level arms, Harry made an unusual adjustment: He started swinging even more. He turned it loose 60% of the time during his 48 games at Double-A, one of the higher rates in all of pro ball. It worked, too, as Harry posted a 140 wRC+ with eight bombs and then was again an above-average hitter following a promotion to Triple-A.
A big season at the plate has done wonders for Harry’s stock, in part because he was already a slick defender. He’s a solid-average shortstop with quick feet, a strong arm, and a knack for making plays at full extension. Average hands and throwing accuracy kept me from getting too crazy with the fielding grade here, but given the versatility — Harry has experience at second base and all over the outfield — you could justify projecting him as a plus defender.
Harry won't have to hit much to help a ballclub, which is good because I'm concerned he won’t. His operation in the box is unconventional. He sometimes loads in part by arching his back as the pitcher prepares to deliver, drifts his front forward, and then puts his full body into his swing in a way that leaves his head bouncing all over the place. He’s often off balance against spin and can’t help but chase all manner of slop well off the plate. Big leaguers aren’t going to have to throw him strikes all that often to get him out, and while Harry has a little pop, he probably isn't going to punish enough mistakes to stay in the lineup with his current approach. He has the ceiling of a super sub if this part of his game matures beyond expectations.

Name: Dexters Peralta
Report:
Despite the fact that he struck out at a 35.7% clip in his second FCL season, I can't totally quit Peralta because his tools are simply too loud. His youth, projection and athleticism made him a notable DSL prospect in 2024 despite his strikeouts. Switch-hitting shortstops — Peralta is a slick defender who is a virtual lock to stay there and could be plus if he stays lean and rangy — with this kind of power are rare, and though his K's remain a horrendous problem, his left-handed power has begun to actualize in a meaningful way. 
Now that said, Peralta might want to give up switch-hitting. His contact rate as a righty was a damning 56% in 2026, while from the left side it was a more workable (though still bad) 65%. His swing is naturally geared for pull and lift as a lefty, and his measureable power numbers from that side (35% hard-hit, 103.7 mph EV90, 107 max) are all multiple grades better than from the right side. Can a singular focus on left-handed hitting facilitate enough improvement for Peralta to sustain his 65% contact rate up the minor league ladder and become a Colson Montgomery type of hitter? He won't turn 20 until July 2027 and will be a six-year minor league free agent when he's only 23. I'd stay on this guy for a while to see what happens between now and then.

Name: Blake Burkhalter
Report:
Last list cycle, I speculated that Burkhalter’s days in the rotation were likely numbered, and that came to fruition in 2026. He was effective in 1-2 inning stints, pitching to a 2.43 ERA across 29.2 Triple-A innings while striking out 10.01 per nine with otherwise strong peripherals. He even made his big league debut, working a single inning in early September.
Neither Burkhalter’s delivery nor his stuff changed much in relief, with one exception. After working with both a slider and a curve in 2025, he was down to a single breaking ball in 2026. It looked pretty sharp, too, a tight 12-6 buckler thrown a few ticks harder than what he had before. I'll guess he calls it a curve — the pitch classification systems do — but it looks like a better, and better commanded, version of the slider he had earlier. Otherwise, he lives in the mid-90s with a carrying fastball, an average cutter, and a sinking change that projects a half tick better than that if he can locate it competitively with greater consistency. While it’s a control-over-command profile, Burkhalter throws plenty of strikes, and the overall package projects comfortably in middle relief.

Name: Jake Cook
Report:
Cook began his college career in the Southern Mississippi bullpen, where he was wild and rarely got on the bump in games. He switched to the outfield prior to his junior season and, despite no significant reps at the plate since high school, flourished there. He hit .350/.436/.468 with 31 walks and just 19 strikeouts in 60 games, a mind-blowing season given the previous two sentences. He’s also an 80 runner and a projectable center fielder, and the overall package enticed Toronto to give him nearly a million bucks out of the 2025 draft. 
While Cook’s offensive production suggested he might hit the ground running in pro ball, it now looks like he'll be in the slow lane. He struck out a lot at Low-A and was barely a league-average hitter there, as a ton of popups limited his ability to put his wheels to work. His rawness on both sides of the ball makes him more of an interesting flier to monitor than a near-term contributor. Still, elite speed is elite speed, and there’s more runway ahead to develop than Cook’s age alone would imply. He’s also a daylight guy for us: Eric likes him a fair bit, and went to bat for him as we kicked around names toward the bottom of the list.

Name: Wilson Rodriguez
Report:
Rodriguez wasn't healthy for big chunks of his first couple seasons in pro ball, and he spent significant time on the complex roster from 2023-2025 just trying to get into a routine and find his footing. Though he only played 30 games at Low-A toward the end of 2025, the Yankees assigned him to High-A Hudson Valley at the start of 2026, and he responded by hitting .259/.379/.427 as an age-appropriate 21-year-old. 
Rodriguez is a selective, sinewy lefty-hitting outfielder with a modest toolset. His swing is geared for lifting pitches at the top of the strike zone, but he struggles to do damage in other locations and settles for a lot of singles. Because he's an average runner with a well below-average arm, his best defensive fit is in left field. Though there's enough happening on offense here to consider Rodriguez an eventual above-replacement player, it's tough to forecast him in a consistent on-roster role unless he continues to get stronger and ends up with more power than I think he'll have at peak.

Name: Cedric De Grandpre
Report:
De Grandpre signed for just shy of $240,000 out of a Florida community college back in 2022. After a promising 2023, he missed all of 2024 recuperating from Tommy John and then was uncharacteristically erratic in his return in 2025. He righted the ship this past year, though, and pitched himself onto the main section of this list after firing 129.2 innings of 4.23 ERA ball, with a 29% strikeout rate and less than a homer per inning allowed across the upper three levels.
De Grandpre works out of an old school, overhead motion. He strides straight, and his drop-and-drive delivery gives him above-average extension and a low release height out of a three-quarters arm slot. While he'll touch 98, his fastballs aren't anything special, low-90s offerings with dead zone tail and sink. He leans heavily on his secondaries, and his good feel for spin and ability to locate a few different breaking balls give him a chance to soak up innings in some kind of lower-impact, multi-inning role. There’s also a path to a more conventional middle relief role if short stints unlock considerably more velocity and allow the fastball to play better in the zone than it has as a starter. The Braves added him to their 40-man roster just prior to publication.

Name: Paul Gutierrez-Contreras II
Report: Gutierrez-Contreras is a strong-bodied 6-foot-3 outfielder who slashed .346/.441/.633 during his draft-eligible sophomore season and then .283/.392/.433 in Tampa after the draft. He executes a simple, gap-to-gap approach with a compact, conservative swing that takes advantage of his strength. It's a coherent, understated style of hitting that produces doubles power. PGC doesn't run all that well and his arm strength is going to limit him to left field, so his overall ceiling is limited, barring a change that unlocks more power.

Name: Dub Gleed
Report:
Gleed was traded from Miami to Toronto at the end of March in exchange for Leo Jiménez. The timing of that deal meant he fell through the cracks of our team lists last cycle, even though he has (and had) the talent for a full write-up.
Gleed is in many ways a modern hitter. He’s trying to lift the ball to the pull side, and he has the open stride and lofted swing that often come with that approach. He registered a 15 degree launch angle and 39.4% groundball rate in 2026, which shows that he’s pretty good at it. Even though Gleed’s bat speed and raw power are just fair, strong pitch recognition and bat-to-ball skills help make it all work. Better stuff looms as a real test, because he’s just not that physical, but the projection here is for him to get to enough power to be dangerous.
Gleed has played both first and third base. On tape, it looks like he has the glove for the hot corner, as you can see him make a bunch of tough pickups on hard grounders and in-between hoppers, but his arm scares me. A lot of his throws are aimed or lobbed, his accuracy is below average, and his release also isn't particularly quick. Oddly, the operation looks worse when he has time, and some of his best and firmest throws come when he has to really make a play. Taken together, he looks more like a guy who fits better in a reserve corner role than in an everyday job.

Name: Isaiah Drake
Report:
Drake is a local kid who signed for just shy of $750,000 in the 2024 draft. A sprained thumb limited him to 68 regular season games in 2026, though he’s healthy again and played in the Arizona Fall League. At High-A, he hit .264/.342/.443, good for a 111 wRC+, while doubling his home run total from 2025.
Drake’s athleticism and swing excite and scare me in roughly equal measure. He’s quick, can steal bases, and has grown into decent power. His cut is janky, though, with no load and a stiff-looking path. He’s made viable rates of contact throughout his career and isn't overly susceptible to any one pitch, which gives him a chance to hit his way into some kind of role. This profile would be a little more exciting if Drake could play center, but he’s barely done so over the past two years and looks more good than great on tape in a corner. As is, he projects as an optionable outfielder who could have a more relevant peak if he maxes out on the power projections above.

Name: Leni Done
Report:
Done is a well-rounded hitter who has performed in rookie ball during each of his two pro seasons, with virtually all of his metrics either holding water or improving in the 2026 FCL. A corner-quality athlete, he isn't overly toolsy, but Done is a fluid in-the-box rotator for his size and covers the top of the strike zone very well. He already has roughly average pull power and is capable of stroking doubles down both foul lines. He isn't the twitchiest, most explosive guy, but he has a balanced offensive skill set and approach. 
Though he has experience at all four infield positions, Done is likely a long-term 3B/1B or range-deficient second baseman. He doesn't have especially good hands, range, or throwing accuracy, and he's a work in progress on defense to say the least. But he's a good enough hitter not to worry about those specifics yet, as he might hit enough to be a big league contributor at lesser infield positions.

Name: Josh Kasevich
Report: After a lost 2025 season, Kasevich enjoyed good health and put up a solid full campaign at Triple-A Buffalo, where he played all over the infield and posted a contact-fueled, league-average batting line. Kasevich has one of the best hit tools in the minor leagues. He can get the bat on anything, and between that and his patient approach, he’s been on base a lot as a professional. He isn't punchless in the box — his hard-hit rate was about 37%, and his 110 mph max EV is only a smidge short of average — but he’s mostly a singles hitter. Defensively, Kasevich is an adequate, if fringy, shortstop. He isn't especially quick or rangy, and compensates instead with reliable hands and accurate throws. He’s a low-variance, big-league-ready utility infielder, and given that he'll be 26 on Opening Day, his window of productivity will most likely occur in his pre-arb years.

Name: Jack Brenner
Report: Brenner signed for just shy of $1.25 million in the 2026 draft, well overslot in the seventh round. He’s a plus athlete with good wheels and a multi-positional background, and the Braves announced him as a catcher. While Brenner didn't make a ton of appearances on the showcase circuit, he made a lot of contact when he did, which is particularly exciting for a cold-weather prep bat. His A-swing has a lot of venom, a fast, looping cut built to do damage to the pull side. Spin and pitches away from him can leave him off balance, perhaps exacerbated by an upright stance. Brenner has years to iron it out, though. What matters now is that he’s a good athlete with a little pop and barrel feel at a premium position. We'll see how it all looks in pro ball this spring.

Name: Stiven Marinez
Report:
Marinez signed a $1.65 million deal at the very end of the 2024 calendar, a couple months after he had turned 17. A lukewarm 2025 debut meant the Yankees kept him in the DSL for a second season in 2026, and he responded by cutting his strikeout rate nearly in half (from 22.4% to 12.4%); he was also sixth in the DSL with 39 stolen bases (at an 85% success rate) and tied for 13th in homers with eight (he hit just one in 2025). 
A medium-framed 5-foot-10, Marinez did a better job of being on time and meeting the baseball over top of the plate in 2026. He's at his best targeting pitches on the inner half, and does most of his damage against pitches middle-in and middle-up. His contact rate (76%) was a grade better than the prior year, and he showed a modest uptick in his power-hitting metrics as well. He has a roughly average hit tool projection and more of a 40- or 45-grade raw power projection, which isn't bad for a potential shortstop. That said, Marinez's defense looked worse than the notes from 2025, with his hands and arm strength on the fringe of what's viable at shortstop. Still, he has good range and is athletic, and he should be developed at short. Realistically, he's a lower-ceiling'd utility infielder, and hangs on to the bottom of the Yankees list as a high-priority follow due to his bonus pedigree and the well-rounded foundation of his offense.

Name: Carson Messina
Report:
Messina was an overslot 12th-round pick in 2024 and, presumably to the disappointment of resident Gamecock Michael Bauman, he signed for $550,000 to forgo his commitment to South Carolina. He was wild but effective in his return from elbow inflammation this year, a malady that cost him just about all of the 2025 season. He generated plenty of grounders, struck out 27.3% of opponents, and registered an ERA just north of 3.00. But he also walked 16.5% of opponents and had a couple of disaster outings where he couldn't escape the first. 
While Messina isn’t the loosest athlete, his delivery is fairly simple, and the guess here is that he'll throw more strikes with experience. The stuff is good enough to stay patient with. Messina touches 98 and he had outings where he sat in the mid-90s this past summer. The fastball plays down from the velo a bit; despite a lot of carry and a short stroke, he's a short, open strider and not particularly deceptive. He can really spin it, though, and the curve, slider, and cutter carved through Low-A bats. It's worth continuing to develop him as a starter for the reps, but in the long run, he projects as a breaking-ball-heavy, mid-to-high-leverage reliever.

Name: Diego Tornes
Report:
Tornes inked a $2.3 million bonus prior to the 2025 season, making him Atlanta’s biggest signing of that year’s international class. He had a solid first season in the DSL, hitting .279/.395/.402 with average raw power, though he didn't homer in his 32 games. He showed up to camp in great shape and even got into a game this past spring, where he worked a walk against a big league reliever.
Unfortunately, that proved to be the high-water mark for Tornes in 2026. A rib issue delayed the start of his season, and lingering effects from that perhaps explain the reduced exit velocities and hard-hit rates he posted, along with a complete inability to drive the ball in games. Either way, Tornes didn’t hit a lick. I still like the athlete, and see both hit skill and a path to plus power, but there’s a lot left unresolved here — Is he a switch-hitter? Can he play center?— and he’s no longer on the fast track to Atlanta. This is a case where the ceiling hasn't changed, but Tornes’s odds of reaching it look dimmer than they did 12 months ago.

Name: Bradley Hanner
Report:
A nice find by Minnesota as a $10,000 second-year junior college pitcher, Hanner's career got off to a delayed start because of the pandemic, which is part of why he was available for Cleveland to select in the minor league phase of the 2022 Rule 5 Draft. A six-year minor league free agent after 2025, Hanner signed with the Yankees and pitched well enough at Scranton throughout 2026 to enter New York's low-leverage bullpen mix in the season's second half. 
Hanner is a bit of a pitch data darling because he creates 20 inches of horizontal movement on his slider and is a low release guy (drop-and-drive lower body, shorter arm action than most sidearmers) whose fastball has natural uphill angle. Neither of those pitches looks quite as nasty as it grades out in the pitch models (Stuff+ loves this dude, for instance), but Hanner has a long track record of striking out at least a batter per inning. He has real-world baseball value as a reliable middle reliever who still has option years left.

Name: José Rodríguez
Report:
You may or may not have known that minor leaguers can still be traded after the deadline. Rodríguez was involved in such a swap, joining the Jays from Los Angeles in exchange for Sebastian Rodriguez.
Rodríguez is a fun watch. He’s got a throwback, ’70s-style delivery where he starts completely closed to the plate, nearly knees himself in the chin as he coils, somehow rocks back even further as his arm stretches toward the ground, and then springs toward home. For Super Smash fans, the load-and-go effect is somewhat reminiscent of watching Samus queue up her arm cannon. What comes out of the arm is pretty interesting, too. Rodríguez will touch 100 mph, albeit with mediocre shape, and both the slider and changeup project as plus offerings.
Unsurprisingly given the delivery, Rodríguez isn't a good strike-thrower. Partly because he’s wild and partly because they can't really hit him, Triple-A hitters have been content to take their walks and have done so in about 14% of their plate appearances over the last two years. That’s too high, even for a guy running enormous whiff rates on two secondaries. He projects as an effectively wild middle reliever, but the risk he’s an often-wild, rarely-effective depth option is pretty high.

Name: Luis Guanipa
Report:
Guanipa was a $2.5 million international signee out of Venezuela in the 2023 class. Despite the bonus, the 20-year-old is neither especially toolsy nor projectable, and the contours to his profile are similar to what they were a year ago. He makes a lot of contact (77% overall, 84% in zone), but it’s not especially authoritative. He tends to swing inside the ball and generates a lot of opposite-field contact. Guanipa has average bat speed and is only able to consistently pull offspeed pitches that hang over the middle or inner part of the plate. His approach and swing decisions are generally solid, but he started chasing more spin off the plate this past year and hardly walked at all after a late-season promotion to High-A.
Defensively, Guanipa’s tape is a mixed bag, with a blend of good reads off the bat and drifty routes that sometimes get him in trouble. He has the look of a guy who can play but not excel in center, and if anything, he looks a half step slower than he did at last check-in. There’s still enough hit skill and defensive versatility for him to grow into a fourth outfielder role, but some of the strongest parts of his game look a little dicier than they did in the low minors, and he’s correspondingly fallen a bit in this update.

Name: Antonio Gomez
Report: Gomez was a high-profile amateur catcher renowned for his arm strength but not his bat. He struggled enough in the lower minors that part of the way through 2025, as he was about to become a six-year minor league free agent, a conversion to the mound began. Gomez re-signed with New York on a minor league deal and pitched in Tampa late in 2026, and then in Arizona during the Fall League. He was sitting 96-98 and touching 100 during that brief window, with an 87-92 mph cutter that lacks bat-missing length. Converted position players who become successful relievers tend to improve pretty quickly. Gomez's arm strength makes him a notable prospect who will hopefully show a true plus secondary pitch sometime in 2027 and end the season in the mix for the Yankees' 40-man roster.

Name: Ty Southisene
Report:
Southisene comes from a family of baseball players, and his brother Tate is a Top 100 prospect in Atlanta’s system. The Cubs paid this Southisene seven figures to steer him away from his commitment to Tennessee. After a solid, if punchless, start to his pro career at the plate, the Blue Jays landed him in this summer’s Kevin Gausman trade. He’s a Toronto type of acquisition: short, twitchy, lot of contact, nice swing, positional versatility up the middle, not much pop. Toronto's player dev group has worked wonders with many a farmhand, but they have an uphill battle to get the slender Southisene to anything beyond 30 game power.
Southisene has good hands and instincts at short, but both his arm and range, particularly in the six-hole, are currently light for the role. The rosy forecast here is that he can become an average defender there as he matures, but I have sources who think that’s a little hot. A lot rides on whether he can do it, as it might be the difference between a long-term utility fit and more of an up-down profile.

Name: Starlyn De La Cruz
Report: De La Cruz signed for $1.2 million in the 2026 international class. He snuck onto our list last cycle as a speedy outfielder with a chance to play a crisp center field, then showed up in pro ball with much more power than we anticipated, 40 grade already. De La Cruz is up 15 pounds from where he was listed, and both that and a swing built to do damage have worked their magic. For how hard he swings, De La Cruz’s feel for contact is pretty good, and he has a patient, mature approach. I'm always leery of swing data in rookie ball, but when a guy can actually lower his chase rate with two strikes, that’s impressive anywhere. The only blemish on his 2026 campaign was that it didn't last very long, as he dislocated his shoulder diving back to first on a pickoff throw in June and missed the rest of the season; he should be ready to go for spring training. While I don't want to get too carried away with a guy who doesn't have a ton of physical projection ahead of him, De La Cruz is an interesting sleeper, and his stock is up year over year.

Name: Omar Alfonzo
Report: Acquired from Pittsburgh as part of the Camilo Doval deal, Alfonzo remains below average in most facets of catching defense, especially his framing, and his offense has tanked since he was promoted to Double-A. He was hitting for plus power (on the surface and under the hood) while he was in hitter-friendly Greensboro, but he was also striking out a lot, which has only become more consequential since he joined the Yankees system. It's too early to completely write off a young player with this kind of left-handed power, but Alfonzo is treading water on defense while his offense backs up, putting him more on the long-term 40-man fringe.

Name: RJ Schreck
Report:
Schreck was lightly recruited out of high school and nearly wound up at MIT before deciding to walk on at Duke. It took a few years, but he hit his way into the Blue Devils lineup and put himself in position to transfer to Vanderbilt after he graduated. He parlayed a strong super-senior season into a low-dollar draft bonus with the Mariners, who quickly flipped him to the Jays in exchange for Justin Turner in 2024. He got stronger seemingly overnight, and a corresponding uptick in power, combined with his patient approach, helped turn Schreck from a nice story into a real prospect. 2026 wasn't quite a lost year for him, but a wrist sprain limited him to 70 games and kept him down in Buffalo. When healthy, he was his usual patient self, though he didn't hit for the same kind of power — raw or game — that he showed in 2025. 
Even before this past season’s middling campaign, Schreck was a divisive player. There is a strong analyst/scout split at work here, and the scouts are mostly underwhelmed. Schreck needs a deep load and a long swing to generate his power, and it takes him a while to get his bat from the launch point to the hitting zone. A long swing and a slow bat is often a deadly combination, one more commonly found in Quad-A hitters than big league run producers.
Defensively, Schreck has occasionally manned center, but he’s a corner outfielder. I tend to be skeptical of corner bats without big pop who derive substantial value from their approach, and I don't really see Schreck as an exception. There are plenty of people throughout the industry who like him quite a bit, and so with a nod to sources whose opinions I respect and value, I'm keeping him up here on the list, even though I think he’s more of an up-down guy with a platoon ceiling than an impactful hitter.

Name: Martires Polanco
Report: Polanco is the top DSL pitcher in this system. He has average size and a fast arm, the latter of which helps him generate mid-90s velo and touch 99. Polanco has the best arm strength of any of Atlanta's complex leaguers, and also the best breaking ball, as his slider flashes plus. There’s a long way to go here, as he isn't throwing a changeup in games yet, he’s a little wild, and he has only worked into the fifth inning a few times. At this level, though, we're mostly looking for athleticism and traits, and Polanco’s are quite good.

Name: Bryce Cunningham
Report: Cunningham's stock is in limbo. His velocity and overall bat-missing ability were both way down in 2026, and his heater got crushed by High-A hitters. Increased reliance on his changeup to navigate outings also made that pitch less of a bat-misser than before. He finished the year with four good starts at Somerset, and Cunningham still has some exciting traits — he generates over seven feet of extension and is a fluid, athletic mover for a big, husky guy — and a great changeup, but he'll grade like a spot starter for as long as his fastball is this vulnerable.

Name: Jake Casey
Report:
The son of former big leaguer Sean Casey, Jake is a departure from the type of hitters Toronto tends to gravitate toward. He’s an athletic, strapping lad with a fast bat, a chance to grow into plus power, and a scary swing that threatens the profile entirely. He’s bottom-hand dominant in the extreme, and he lands late in a way that seems to contribute to his problems adjusting off the fastball. The good and the bad were on display in 2026, when he socked 12 homers and posted a 129 wRC+ in 57 High-A games, but also struck out 27.8% of the time with huge whiff rates against all types of secondaries.
Defensively, Casey has seen time across the outfield. He’s a fit in center, where he has enough speed for the job and isn't afraid of the ball. His arm strength is a little light, though he gets rid of the ball pretty quickly. As a late bloomer out of a small, cold-weather school, it’s worth staying patient on the tools here even if the data is pretty scary. He has a fourth outfielder’s ceiling.

Name: Raudy Reyes
Report:
Teams are often leery of giving big bonuses to pitchers in the international market, but the Braves rolled the dice on Reyes and spent $1.8 million to see if they could turn elite arm strength into impact pitching. After a walk-and-strikeout-heavy DSL debut, the big guy blew out in a bullpen session just a couple weeks into the spring, and missed all of 2026 after undergoing Tommy John surgery. You can thus add the injury to the pile of concerns covered in last year’s report, which is reproduced here: 
Reyes lulls batters into a false sense of security with his languid delivery. He has a slow leg rise and a low-effort motion that produces some of the easiest upper-90s velocity you'll find. His fastball touches 101 and comes with an average of 18 inches of vertical break. He can spin it, too, most apparently in a visual way with his sharp and slurvy curve, but he’s also got a hard and tight slider that ran roughshod over DSL bats.
All of this sounds promising, but Reyes isn't on the fast track. He isn't a great athlete, and he’s having a ton of trouble getting to release consistently. He’s all over the place with everything, and so while nobody could hit him (20 hits and 35 strikeouts in 27 innings), nobody can really catch him yet either (10 wild pitches, 29 walks, two poor hit batsmen). He’s big and young and deserves time to grow into his frame and limbs. With stuff like this, you can live with even well below-average control in some capacity. He’s projected here as a late-inning reliever, though the variance bars are almost as big as Reyes himself. Atlanta should give him every chance to start, as his ceiling is sky high if he can find a way to throw strikes.

Name: Franyer Herrera
Report: It took Herrera a long time to leave the DSL, and when he finally did so in 2025, the Yankees moved him to the bullpen. In 2026, he was shifted back into a starting role and promoted to Hudson Valley, where each of Herrera's three pitches missed bats at an above-average rate even though he only sits 91 mph. Herrera is athletic and has a pretty delivery. Both of his secondary pitches — a mid-80s changeup that has always been the best of his mix, and an 80-85 mph slider with depth that stems from his vertical arm slot — are at least average, and Herrera throws strikes with each of them at a better rate than you might think given his 2026 walk rate (12.4%). He's a velo uptick away from having a breakout, which always seems like a possibility in this system. For now, he looks like a future spot starter.

Name: Nick Goodwin
Report: Goodwin has exceeded my expectations. When I first saw him a couple of years ago, he was a punchless shortstop who had a lot of trouble catching up to fastballs in the upper half of the zone, an impression that I retained after he repeated High-A in 2025. At the upper levels in 2026, Goodwin had a productive campaign, hitting .263/.363/.464 with limited drop off after a promotion to Triple-A. The combination of surprising strength development (though not traditionally projectable, he’s added several ticks to both his max and 90th-percentile EVs over the past couple of years) and a couple of small mechanical adjustments (he’s turned a double toe tap into a more traditional lift-and-stride and shortened his load) have helped Goodwin develop fringy power while also making more contact. The window of the zone where he can reliably do damage is still narrow, and you can get him out with good spin, but he looks like a competitive big league hitter. It’s a credit to both the org’s dev competencies and the player’s work that he’s gotten to this point. Defensively, Goodwin is capable at short, with decent hands and a very quick release. He projects as a utility infielder.

Name: Cole Dennis
Report: Dennis was selected out of a Jacksonville high school in the fourth round of the 2026 draft and signed for $523,275. We think that’s a pretty nice piece of business for the Braves. Dennis sat 92-95 with a carrying fastball in starts during the regular season, and his velocity was up a little bit at the 2026 Draft Combine. His power breaking ball flashes plus, and he already has decent feel for killing spin on his changeup. He’s a strong kid, close to maturity, and he has a repeatable, up-tempo delivery. It wouldn't shock me if he breaks camp in the Low-A rotation and, provided that he’s able to hold his stuff and throw strikes in a pro environment, he could be in line for a re-evaluation as early as the end of the spring.

Name: Richard Matic
Report:
Matic signed for a little less than $1 million in the 2024 international period. The huge corner infielder was young for the class and needed a sophomore spin through the DSL in 2025, one he passed with flying colors, hitting .336/.487/.566 with five bombs in 46 games. In his first taste of domestic pro ball in 2026, Matic slashed .283/.394/.439 and got some exposure to first base, which might be his ultimate defensive destination due to his size and lack of mobility. 
Built like a middle linebacker at about 235 pounds, Matic has meaningful (albeit unprojectable) power. His swing has a natural inside-out tendency, and a lot of his contact is sprayed to right field even though he often catches the baseball in front of the plate. He's shown enough ability to pull pitches on the inner third that this isn't a red flag issue, but it's probably part of why Matic has just nine home runs in 150 career games despite wielding good power. Vulnerable to breaking stuff away from him, Matic has run contact rates in the 74-76% range as a pro and struck out at a 23.1% clip in 2026. That isn't bad, but it also isn't particularly scintillating for a corner infielder without much strength projection. Maikel Franco is a fair comp for what Matic projects to be at maturity.

Name: CJ Van Eyk
Report: Van Eyk’s prospect stock has yo-yo’d considerably throughout his professional career. Here and there, he looked like a no. 4-caliber starter with average arm strength and a plus curve. He’s had to battle through a lot, though, as he’s undergone Tommy John, seen his velocity fluctuate, and moved in and out of various minor league rotations. More often, he’s looked like a no. 5 or 6 starter. In 2026, more than six years after draft day, he finally ascended to the majors, where he made a handful of appearances in various roles. His long-term projection is for more of that kind of thing, wearing a few different hats in an up-down role.

Name: Zach Royse
Report: Royse was Atlanta’s seventh-rounder in the 2025 draft. He’s a downhill thrower adept at pounding the glove-side corner, mostly with his fastball and slider. The latter flashes above average and headlines a mix of otherwise average and fringy stuff. For a guy who has pretty good touch and feel, the lack of a changeup is conspicuous in its absence. If he can find one, he has a backend starter’s ceiling. More likely, Royse stands a chance of finding work in some type of middle relief role as he transitions to shorter stints.

Name: Andrew Gonzalez
Report: Gonzalez signed for $375,000 rather than head to Texas Tech. He's a physically mature corner infield prospect with a really sweet-looking lefty swing, one that features loft and power created in a short mechanical distance. Gonzalez wasn't a frequent showcase presence and only played in a Bridge League setting after the draft, so his hit tool is about as black a box as there is in this system. But he has meaningful lefty power and overt physicality, no more or less volatile a hitter than the DSL standout or two in the org.

Name: Landon Maroudis
Report: Maroudis signed for $1.5 million out of high school back in 2023. He's a svelte 6-foot-3 with a drop-and-drive delivery and low release height for his size. A year further removed from the internal brace procedure that cost him most of the 2024 season, Maroudis found the strike zone much more reliably in 2026. The trouble was that hitters tattooed most of what he threw, and his ERA was over 6.00 at High-A. Visually, his fastball, curve, and slider all flash above average, and he'll sporadically show feel for locating in productive areas (his change has a similar pattern but is even less far along). But he isn't able to do so consistently, and so while he has a path to contributing in some kind of role, his execution will need to take a sizable leap forward to get there. Maroudis is one where a couple of sources who saw him this year liked him, and their views helped shade him up from the Honorable Mentions onto the main list.

Name: Ryne Barker
Report: The Braves signed Barker for an overslot $700,000 out of an Arizona high school. On the limited video available, he looks like a good hitter, with a short, direct swing and a little verve in his hands. He’s pretty good at adjusting off the fastball, too. In more ways than one, this is an odd profile. Older high school draftees tend to be less projectable than their peers for obvious reasons, but Barker himself is green, and he has a tapered frame that looks ripe for future growth, both of which are exciting for a guy with hit skill but underdeveloped power. Defensively, the path ahead isn't clear. Barker played a lot of third base as an amateur — odd for a high schooler with speed and a good arm — and Atlanta's plan to work him in at short in 2027 adds another wrinkle here. It all makes Barker a high-variance player of an unusual flavor, one whose game I suspect won't really come into focus until we get to see him in professional games.

Name: Cesar Lopez
Report: Lopez is a stocky catcher who takes a very healthy hack for his size, and does so without sacrificing so much contact as to be concerned about his overall future as a hitter yet. The 17-year-old slashed .286/.439/.421 in his DSL debut. He rotates really well for a little guy and posted a 76% contact rate despite a deep, aggressive load. No 17-year-old is a great defensive catcher, and Lopez only caught 22 games in 2026, limiting looks. He popped in the 1.96 to 2.00 second range on the throws he was able to successfully send to second base and framed low pitches well, though DSL umpires are often eager to call strikes to keep games moving. Though he isn't especially projectable, Lopez is precocious and plays the position that requires the greatest inventory industry-wide. He's a deep sleeper who seems likely to repeat the DSL in 2027 because of the Yankees' tendency not to promote guys after just one year down there.

Name: Josh Stephan
Report: Stephan signed with Texas as an undrafted free agent in 2020 and was dealt to Toronto, along with Josh Smith, at the deadline in exchange for Adam Macko. Since then, the righty has advanced slowly but steadily through the minors as a command-and-control-oriented starter with a couple of good breaking balls but below-average arm strength and fastball shape. After a rough ride in both Triple-A leagues, it’s starting to look like his stuff is a little too soft to reliably turn over a lineup multiple times. Time and again in 2026, he'd have outings where he missed barrels and drew chases on his slider and cutter the first time through the order, only to run into trouble later on as hitters stopped biting. Stephan can still help, perhaps in a multi-inning role, maybe in a more traditional relief role if he gains a few ticks in short stints. But, barring an unexpected velo surge, he now projects as a lower-leverage relief fit or spot starter rather than a backend guy.

Name: Rolddy Muñoz
Report:
Though Muñoz bettered his Triple-A production from 2025 and again earned a cup of coffee with the Braves, he wasn't quite the same guy. His fastball, regularly in the upper 90s and touching triple digits in 2025, sat 94-97 this past year and got whacked. There was a corresponding dip in the velo and nastiness of his slider, so while that pitch still missed a ton of bats, it wasn't quite the same top-of-the-scale weapon that earned a present 70 on the last edition of this list. 
Arm strength is a fickle friend, which is troubling in Muñoz’s case, because he’s on a sensitive part of the velo spectrum. His fastballs don't have very good shape, and even though he’s not a high-effort thrower, his cross-body delivery and long arm path produce below-average command and control. That’s bearable with plus-plus arm strength, but if Muñoz’s is just 60-grade over the long haul, he'll be more of an up-and-down guy than a consistently rostered middle reliever. The pitch grade projections above account for the possibility of a bounce back, while the topline FV reflects the uncertainty that he might not.

Name: Luis Velasquez
Report:
Velasquez is a wild little righty reliever whose arm is too fast for him to control. He returned from elbow surgery in May of 2026, made five rehab appearances in Tampa, then spent the rest of the year split between Hudson Valley and Somerset. Combined, Velasquez worked 31 innings and had a career-best 10.8% walk rate. He also pitched a couple of times in the Dominican Winter League prior to list publication. 
Velasquez sits 97. He has a plus slider, and has improved his tailing low-90s changeup. The changeup may be a way for him to throw an acceptable rate of strikes, because his fastball and slider feel both remained crude coming out of rehab. Velasquez's arm speed and secondary pitch quality are exciting enough to value him as a prospect even though he currently has unusable control.

Name: Dameury  Pena
Report: Pena was the third piece in the return package for Jeff Hoffman. For what feels like the umpteenth time this list, we're talking about a little guy with bat control, not much power, and less defensive versatility than you’d like. At the plate, his setup reminds me of Jean Segura’s. While he doesn't have that kind of a hit tool (or power), Pena has short levers, moves the bat around the zone well, and can adjust off the fastball. He struck out in only 7.1% of his plate appearances in 2026 and has some of the highest contact rates in the system. With the glove, Pena is rangy enough for second, but his hands aren't great. He lacks the arm for the left side of the infield or the speed you’d like to see in center. There’s enough bat-to-ball skill to stay on him, but unless he really hits or his feel for defense comes late, Pena looks like he'll be a tricky roster fit.

Name: Herick Hernandez
Report: Hernandez reached Gwinnett as an effectively wild starter. He’s a good example of how an easy delivery doesn’t always translate to strikes. His motion is low maintenance, and a long arm path and slight spinal tilt are minor nitpicks in an operation that otherwise looks pretty clean. His command is better than you’d think looking at the numbers, as he’s pretty reliably able to work with his fastball up and locate his spinny breaking balls down or below the zone. Still the lack of strikes is enough of a problem that, even though he’s started throughout his career, he’s likely ticketed for relief. The projection is for his carrying, low-to-mid-90s fastball and above-average, two-plane slider to give lefties enough fits to play some kind of role, possibly as a full-time second southpaw in the ‘pen.

Name: Thomas  Balboni Jr.
Report: Balboni is a sidearm reliever who experienced a two-tick velo bump in 2024 and now has uncommon velo for a low-slot guy. He was traded from San Diego to New York for Brandon Lockridge when the Padres badly needed outfield depth that summer, and then blew out and had elbow surgery, which kept him out for all of 2025. In a 2026 season spent mostly at Hudson Valley, Balboni was back and healthy, sitting 92-96 with uphill angle and tail that allows his fastball to sneak above barrels at a nearly elite clip. Balboni is still searching for a consistently good breaking ball. He'll throw some curveballs as slow as 82 mph and some cutters as hard as 91, but he didn't throw any of his breakers more than 100 times total throughout 2026; he was a 65% fastball guy on his way to a career-best 3.82 ERA. He's still more of a sleeper than anything else, but he could be a suitable middle reliever who debuts in the next two or three seasons.

Name: Sam Shaw
Report:
Shaw is one of a few Canadians lurking in the Blue Jays system. He grew up in British Columbia and mashed for a month in his backyard of Vancouver this past summer, where he hit .239/.427/.535 in 21 games for the Canadians. As was the case in 2025, injuries limited Shaw’s playing time in 2026. A blood clot in his shoulder cost him the first couple months of the season, and then he went down for the year in July after sustaining an unspecified injury. 
Despite the unexpected power surge, Shaw is a hit-tool oriented batter. He makes an above-average rate of contact and rarely expands the zone, in part because he doesn't swing much at all. When he does turn it loose, he’s direct to the ball and the way he can flatten his swing path facilitates contact throughout the zone. His raw power is well below average, and at his size, will likely remain so. Defensively, Shaw is versatile, if not spectacular. His reads and routes are adequate in center, though his speed fits much better in a corner. He has some second base on his CV as well, though none this past year. His ceiling is as an OBP-over-power fourth outfielder who can stand in center occasionally.

Name: Dixon Williams
Report:
Williams signed for just shy of $500,000 in the 2025 draft. He hit well at High-A Rome in 2026, with 22 homers, 31 steals, and a 113 wRC+, albeit with more strikeouts than you’d like to see. He has an aesthetically pleasing lefty uppercut swing and projects to develop above-average power. Swing-and-miss is probably going to be a problem, though, as he’s often front-footed by all manner of secondaries and he doesn't cover the top rail well against good fastballs.
Defensively, Williams is a jack-of-all-trades type, and he saw time at first, second, and third base in 2026, as well as in left and center, and he even manned short a little bit at East Carolina. He’s pretty good all over, too, as his speed lets him run down a lot of balls in the outfield, and he looks comfortable ranging in both directions on the infield. His arm is too light for regular work on the left side of the infield, but he can play there in a pinch. The power, speed, and defensive versatility give him a lot of paths to some kind of roster fit, and he has a super-utility ceiling if my concerns about contact prove overblown.

Name: Chase Hampton
Report: There have been times since Hampton turned pro when his stuff has been up, mostly in 2023 when his heater resided in the 93-96 mph range and he showed good  breaking balls. At others times, though, it has been down or Hampton has been hurt, which was the case for the bulk of the last three seasons. A flexor tendon strain and a strained groin limited his 2024 output, then Hampton blew out in February 2025 and needed Tommy John, which he returned from in 2026. His stuff was down (sitting 91), and Hampton was DFA'd late in the season. He hopped around waivers (Washington, St. Louis, Baltimore, New York again) but has never pitched for anyone but the Yankees. He's purely a bounce back candidate at this point, one who once looked like a no. 4/5 starter.

Name: Silvano Hechavarria
Report:
Hechavarria is a 23-year-old Cuban righty who signed for about $250,000 in 2024. He’s a loose athlete with good body control and a clean, if slightly long, circular arm swing. As with many strike-throwers with no dominant out pitch, the juiced ball was unkind to Hechavarria in 2026. Despite no real deterioration in the quality of his offerings, his HR/9 more than doubled from 2025 (he again split time between Low- and High-A). The obvious inference is that Hechavarria’s stuff probably won't be crisp enough to turn over major league lineups multiple times.
There’s still enough touch and feel here to project Hechavarria as a big leaguer. He’s adept at locating his fastball at the top of the zone, can run his slider on and off the plate, and, most impressively, has a knack for pulling the string on the change in just the right spot to miss lefty barrels. At this point, though, he looks more like a lower-leverage, one-time-through guy than a potential rotation piece.

Name: Drue Hackenberg
Report: After a disastrous 2025, Hackenberg righted the ship this year. He still got hit a bit in Triple-A, but he aced an early-season repeat assignment in Columbus and struck out 21.9% of the hitters he faced in Gwinnett. The big change was that the righty used his best pitch significantly more often than in 2025, as his curveball usage jumped from 18% to nearly 30%. Leaning into that further could be helpful, as the more hitters have to sit on the deuce, the more he'll be able to tunnel and hide his otherwise mediocre fastball. While Hackenberg has good feel for spin, he had a tough time getting hitters to chase the slider in previous seasons, and he mothballed the pitch in 2026. Though Hackenberg has started throughout his career, his limited arsenal, spin-heavy path forward, and below-average strike-throwing all suggest his future is in relief. He projects as a spin-to-win righty reliever who can flex in and out of multi-inning assignments.

Name: Adrian Pinto
Report:
Pinto is a short, somewhat squat second baseman with surprising physical tools for a player of his stature. He's a good defender at the keystone, with enough arm for the job. He has even played a little center field in recent years, so there's versatility as well. At the plate, Pinto has roughly average power. While he needs a big swing to get to it, his mid-to-upper-70s contact rate is just fine, particularly because he has no obvious vulnerability to spin or high heat. Like Victor Arias, though, Pinto's big cut may be limiting his barrel control and with it a chance to tap into that power regularly.
The other big issue here is injuries, as Pinto again missed significant time in 2026. He's an all-gas, no-brakes type of player, and he's Buxton'd his way into several significant maladies: rib issues and a hamstring strain in 2022, quad strains in 2023, various injuries for a couple of years, and then more rib problems in 2026. All told, he's played in just 234 games across six minor league seasons. On tools, Pinto projects as a quality reserve, and one could argue that he's a "young" 24-year-old given his lack of reps. From a valuation perspective, though, it's hard to list him any higher than this until he proves he can stay on the field for an extended period of time.

Name: Luis Vargas
Report: Vargas is a relief-only prospect who reached Triple-A in 2026. His stuff is clearly big league quality. He'll touch the upper 90s with his fastball and pair it with a hammer of a mid-80s slider, a buckling north-south bender that generated a huge miss rate at Double-A. Vargas’ lack of feel for location precludes a higher grade here. He has a high-effort motion with torque and an enormous recoil at finish, which gives him a tantalizing but often frustrating blend of a chase-heavy mode of attack and bad command. While there’s a little upside if he can find a way to hit the box more often, Vargas projects as an up-down guy who flashes more on occasion.

Name: Jesus Cova
Report:
After missing the 2025 season recovering from Tommy John, Cova was a DSL standout in 2026. Working in mostly three- to four-inning starts, he efficiently chewed through opponents and finished the year by allowing just one earned run and two walks in his last 20 innings.
Cova is a sturdy six feet tall. He has good body control, a repeatable delivery, and a compact arm swing. He throws a bunch of strikes with decent stuff, headlined by a low-to-mid-90s fastball that touches 97 with plus or better tail. He’s also got decent feel to spin a couple of breaking balls, and while nothing misses a ton of bats yet, he has a shapely arsenal with a strike-throwing foundation. He isn't especially physically projectable, but given his feel for spin, there could be a lot of runway to play with shapes. At the very least, Cova's blend of arm strength and control gives him a chance to develop into a guy who can manage contact and generate groundballs.

Name: Jose Perdomo
Report:
Perdomo’s 2026 season practically ended before it began. In his second game of the year, he hit a line drive to the pitcher and slipped on his way out of the box. It was initially reported as a knee tweak, but he was soon placed on the 60-day IL, and he didn't appear in a game the rest of the way. It’s a terrible blow for a player who, in part because he’s already missed the bulk of one pro season with a hamstring injury, hasn't yet been able to live up to his immense amateur prospect billing. With no new information to report, he slides to the bottom of the list, and his report from prior to the season has been reproduced here:
Perdomo signed for $5 million in the 2024 class, the highest bonus ever inked by a Venezuelan player. He played just eight games while battling hamstring injuries in his first season, then endured a rocky 2025 campaign on the Florida complex, where he hit .223/.275/.270. He was signed in large part for his feel to hit, and while a 79% contact rate is decent for an 18-year-old in the FCL, it isn't awesome, particularly if it comes without power and with a tendency to chase stuff off the plate. Defensively, even though he’s played nothing but shortstop thus far, the stiffness in Perdomo’s lower half could force him off the position, which external sources think will happen eventually. It’s not what you want to see when you give all of your bonus pool to one guy.
